247. **N0b's five readings: the candidate set `E` keeps §17.176 (2)'s facts until N4a, which widens it to every managed type and re-records the baseline; miss reasons wait for N3 and never live in `stats()`; recomputing `opt::owned` over the snapshot read back as Core meets §17.176 (2); a remove's untested path copies are neither attempts nor misses until N3 adds the test; the allocation-bound WASM cells must not move at the 0.2.0 window beyond noise (`86262eff`..`4ee9e954`, ABI 1.3.0, `sakura_abi_version` `0x010400`; §17.176, §17.229 (1); REQUESTS 2026-10-19 N0b; round 27).** Facts: `stats()` appends `reuse_attempts`, `reuses`, `borrow_candidates` and `borrows` after `restarts` (120 bytes; the eleven 1.2 counters keep their offsets); every uniqueness test of an owned `List`/`Map`/`Set` update goes through `Rt::reusable`, counted per wrapper and per node on the path; a `Dup` is marked `DupCandidate` when the reference stays live after a call to a read-only builtin (`opt::owned::BORROWS`) or a direct def whose summary borrows the parameter, and `rt_dup_candidate` counts it at run time; the summary tracks collections, carriers and functions, so `String.length(s)` with `s` live after is a `Dup`/`Drop` pair not counted; `sakura_core_snapshot::convert::back` reads a snapshot back as Core, tested as `convert`'s exact inverse on 243 programs, and `sakura_lir` runs `sakura_core::opt::owned` itself over it, the JS and LIR `--dump owned` agreeing on every corpus program; `Map.remove`/`Set.remove` copy their HAMT index path with no uniqueness test (ABI §10 says so); the LIR print snapshots change only `dup` → `dup.candidate`, hand-audited fixtures reconcile each counter, `bench_counters.txt` holds the baseline with the 1.2 counters unchanged, and no WASM code path changed beyond the counter increments; `4ee9e954` fixes `no_wasi`'s reading of a trapped import after N1a moved it. Decision: (1) **`E` stays as built at N0b**: the counter's definition is "executed `Dup`s the LIR marked" and the marking is what the facts the LIR has can justify; a LIR-level "never consumes" fact for every managed type is N4a's first commit (the builtin table already says which builtins only read; a direct def's "never consumes" for scalars-in-boxes, strings and records falls out of the same summary once it tracks them), landed as a marking change before the convention changes, with `bench_counters.txt` re-recorded in that commit as the baseline §17.176 (4)'s bar is read against; ABI §10's sentence gains "the set of marked sites may grow in a later version; a benchmark record's `abi_version` names it". M5b. (2) **Miss reasons are N3's** and, when built, are a separate debug-only export (`stats_reasons`, or `SAKURA_WASM_STATS`'s JSON line gaining a `reasons` object in a debug build) and never fields of `stats()`, whose layout is the same in every build; §17.176 (1)'s "miss reasons in a debug build only" is read that way. Two of the four reasons exist only with tokens, so a reason set now would be half a vocabulary. (3) **Confirmed, and preferred.** §17.176 (2) asked for recomputation from the committed snapshot with one implementation and a parity dump; reading the snapshot back as Core and running the pass is one implementation where `direct.rs` is two, the snapshot stays fact-free (§17.149 (2)), and `back`'s exact-inverse test over the corpus is the condition that keeps it honest and stays in CI. §13.2's "facts in the LIR" sentence is read as "recomputed by the Core pass over the snapshot read back". (4) **Not counted now.** An attempt is an executed uniqueness test (§17.176 (1)); a copy nobody tested is neither, and a miss invented from a path length would make `reuse_rate` depend on which operations happened to be instrumented. N3's in-place delete adds the test, and those copies become attempts and hits or misses there; `bench/deltas.md`'s row for `map_set` and any remove-heavy program names that as the reason attempts rise at N3's first window. ABI §10's sentence stands as written. (5) **Confirmed.** No emitted WASM instruction changed beyond the counter calls, so at the first window after N0b, which is the 0.2.0 window, the allocation-bound set (`nbody`, `sieve`, `spectral_norm`, `rbtree`, `binary_trees`, `deltablue`) reads within noise of the `v0.1.0` baseline on the WASM lane, and the counters' record is `bench_counters.txt`; a move beyond noise is reported with its cause named (the candidates are WS-P13b's facts reaching the LIR through (3), or row 31's stubs), never blessed as N0b's, and `deltablue`'s WASM cell is read under §17.235 (4) in any case. Why: a counter's value is only evidence if its definition does not move under it; one implementation of a fact is a parity test for free; a window reads what changed and names what moved. Rejected: a wider `E` now (a baseline the N4 bar would be read against would then be N0b's accident); reasons in `stats()` (layout per build); counting remove copies as misses (not tests). Performance: none beyond §17.176's four increments. Changed: ABI §10 (one sentence on the marked set; Opus with N4a), plan `m5-native.md` (N0b done, N4a's first commit, N3's remove test), §17.245 (N0b is landed, not M5b). Impact: Opus (N3, N4a, M5b), Astra (`bench/deltas.md` at the 0.2.0 window).

248. **Windows x64 and Intel macOS ship in `v0.1.0`: the release matrix is `packaging/targets.json`, one matrix per tag, no row withheld; every row's claim level for the version is read from `verify-published.yml`, so C's exit moves from `v0.2.0` to the first tag whose published smoke is green on the C rows (changelog agent's question 1; §17.227 (3), (5); §17.180; round 28).** Facts: `targets.json` has five rows and `release.yml`'s plan step emits the whole file as the build and smoke matrix; the last dry run on `main` (`39199739466`, at `e20d941c`) built and install-smoked all five rows green, Windows and Intel included; `verify-published.yml` already carries a `windows-2025` row (`install.ps1` by URL, npm) and a `macos-15-intel` row (installer, npm, brew); the Darwin signing job signs both inventory binaries; `release.py accept` runs the P4 list plus the MCP and LSP `initialize` round trips, and the `core.autocrlf=true` `fmt --check` case of §17.227 (1) is not in it; the install page says Windows and Intel Mac are "coming in v0.2.0", written before P5 and P6 landed; plan `road-to-1.0.md` P8 names `v0.2.0` as "the first release carrying the C archives", an estimate from round 24, while §17.227 (5) defines a stage's exit as the first published-install smoke green on every row of the first release that carries its archives, whichever tag that is. Decision: (1) **Ship them.** The matrix a tag builds is the inventory file at that commit; withholding rows would need a filter that does not exist, written on tag day, to keep back archives whose dry run is green, and would make the inventory and the release disagree. (2) **Claim level by the same rule as every other row**: at the tag no row is supported for 0.1.0; after `verify-published.yml` on `0.1.0` a green row is **supported** for 0.1.0 and a red row is not, stated per row on the install page with the run URL; the notes' sentence ("called supported for this version only after the published-install smoke passes") already says this and stays. A red C row on 0.1.0 is not a P1 release defect (it was never supported) and does not touch the published assets: the page says "published for 0.1.0; its published-install check failed on <row> (<run>); fixed forward", and C's exit waits for the next tag. A red A or B row stays a P1 as §17.227 (3) says. (3) **C's exit is the first tag with both C rows green**, `v0.1.0` if tomorrow's run is; P8 reads so. (4) **The missing `autocrlf` case** of §17.227 (1) is owed on the Windows row (Sol, after the tag, before `v0.2.0`): until it is in, the Windows "supported" line says what was run (installer, npm, the P4 list, MCP, LSP) and not more; the proof-cache limitation (P7) stays stated. (5) **The install page and the `0.1.0` CHANGELOG line** ("explicit Windows/Intel Mac v0.2.0 availability") are rewritten before the tag to "published for 0.1.0; supported once its published-install check is green" (Astra, docs only), and after the run to the result. Why: the evidence that makes a platform supported is the run on the public bytes, which exists only after a tag; delaying the archives to 0.2.0 buys no evidence and keeps two runners' worth of green work in a drawer. Rejected: a per-tag matrix override (code nobody needs); shipping the C archives unlisted (an asset nobody is told about is still an asset); calling C "expected to work" at the tag (that level is for OSes with no hosted runner, §17.227 (3)). Performance: none. Changed: plan `road-to-1.0.md` P8 and timeline row C (this round), install page (Astra), CHANGELOG line (Astra). Impact: Astra (page and changelog line before the tag; per-row result after the run), Sol (the `autocrlf` case; the run and its URL), the owner (nothing new: the same `verify-published.yml` dispatch at close-out).

249. **The 0.1.0 notes and flags: "a pre-1.0 preview" with the no-promise sentence pointing at RFC 0001 and STABILITY.md, never "pre-alpha"; the GitHub pre-release flag and the npm dist-tag follow the version string, so `v0.1.0` is a release marked latest and published to npm `latest`, and only a version with a pre-release identifier (`-alpha.N`, `-rc.N`) is a GitHub prerelease under that identifier's dist-tag (changelog agent's question 2; §17.228 (3); round 28).** Facts: `release.py release_notes` says "a pre-alpha release… Nothing beyond the versioned diagnostic schema and the fixture formats is stable"; `release.yml` runs `gh release create --prerelease --latest=false` unconditionally and `npm publish --tag alpha` with a comment "never the `latest` dist-tag"; §17.228 (3) decided `latest` moves to `v0.1.0` when it publishes; `install.sh` takes `--version` and never resolves `releases/latest`; the CHANGELOG's own header calls 0.1.0 "the first non-alpha preview" with "no stability promise yet… if the owner accepts [RFC 0001], its promises begin at `v0.2.0`"; SemVer defines a pre-release as a version with a hyphenated identifier, and `0.1.0` has none. Decision: (1) **Wording.** The template's first paragraph reads: "Sakura Lang {ver}, a pre-1.0 preview release from commit {commit}. There is no stability promise yet: RFC 0001 proposes the guarantees and, if the owner accepts it, they begin at v0.2.0; STABILITY.md lists what each contract covers today." The rest of the template stands (targets with the supported-only-after sentence, signing, Node 26, Z3, install, the CHANGELOG link). The same two sentences are the rule for every 0.x tag until the RFC is accepted, after which they say which contracts are stable from which version. (2) **Flags from the version string** (`release.py` already parses the pre-release identifier for its version checks): a version without an identifier is created with `--latest=true` and no `--prerelease`, and its npm packages publish under `latest`; a version with one is `--prerelease --latest=false` and publishes under the identifier's first word as the dist-tag (`alpha`, `rc`). `--verify-tag` and the environment approvals stay; the job name "Publish GitHub prerelease" becomes "Publish GitHub release". Owner Sol (`release.yml`, `release.py`, one commit, and `docs/release.md` §6's two sentences in the same commit), before the tag: it is release tooling, compiles no product, and the tag run is the first that exercises it, so the dry run on `main` after it must be green on every row first. Why: the pre-release flag and the dist-tag are statements about the version string, which SemVer already defines, and the readiness statement belongs in the notes and STABILITY.md where it can say exactly what is promised; a 0.x line whose every tag is flagged pre-release makes the flag say nothing, and a `/releases/latest` that resolves to nothing while 0.1.0 exists is a worse answer than 0.1.0. Rejected: flagging every 0.x tag pre-release until 1.0 (the flag stops meaning anything); keeping npm on `alpha` for 0.1.0 (contradicts §17.228 (3) and the install page's plain command); "beta" (the project has no beta stage, §17.225). Performance: none. Changed: `docs/release.md` §6 (Sol, with the code), the notes template. Impact: Sol.

250. **What `v0.1.0` points at: the candidate SHA on `main`, after the preparation commit, with one fully green `ci.yml` run on that exact head; never the exit commit. The window benches the milestone's exit commit and the tag ships the product at tag time, and the two are different commits by design. Between the preparation commit and the tag push nothing lands on `main`. `V8006`, the `[targets]` removal and every post-exit commit ship in 0.1.0 (changelog agent's questions 3 and 4; §17.228 (2), §17.238 (2), (4), §17.240 (4), `docs/release.md` §3 and §5; round 28).** Facts: `main` is 70 commits past `dee11301` at writing: row 30 (security), the Windows test fixes, Intel and Windows packaging, `V8005`, `V8006` with the `[targets]` removal, WS-P13b, row 31, the exhaustiveness index, N0b's counters, trace batching, N1b and N2 native work behind the feature, the JSON baseline and contracts job, the docs and the `0.1.0` CHANGELOG; §17.240 (4) already ruled that a perf commit lands when its conditions are met, that the window benches the pinned commit and that the next window reads the commit; `release.py prepare` writes the version into the workspace in a preparation commit and `release.yml` refuses a tag whose version differs from the workspace's, so a tag can only point at or after that commit; `docs/release.md` §5 says the tag must peel to the approved SHA; CI runs on `main` cancelled each other all afternoon, so no fully green run on the newest head has been read since the Windows fixes (handoff §8). Decision: (1) **The tag points at the candidate SHA**: `main`'s head after the preparation commit, the SHA `release.py prepare` recorded and the owner approves against the dry run's inventory. For every baseline release the rule is the same: the window benches the milestone's exit commit in its own worktree (§17.238 (4)), the blessed baseline carries that commit, and the tag points at the candidate SHA on `main`. (2) **The exit commit is not a tag candidate**: it lacks row 30, the Windows fixes, the C packaging, `V8005`, the release tooling fixes and the changelog, and its workspace version is the alpha's. (3) **Freeze from the preparation commit to the tag push**: nothing lands on `main` in between, so the green `ci.yml` run the tag needs (one run, every job, on that head; the nightly or a `gh workflow run ci.yml --ref main` counts) is on the candidate SHA and is not cancelled by a later push; the freeze is hours, and agents queue their pushes in their worktrees. (4) **`V8006` and `[targets]` ship in 0.1.0**, Breaking as the changelog says: §17.239's "before `v0.2.0`" was a deadline and §17.246's "after the window" was superseded by §17.240 (4); a manifest that is not valid is reported by `check` as a diagnostic from 0.1.0 on, which is what the alpha.1 → 0.1.0 migration section is for. Nothing on `main` is pulled back for the tag. (5) **What 0.1.0 claims about performance**: nothing numeric (the changelog says so); the landed-not-accepted commits (WS-P13b, row 31, `V8006`, the index) are read at the 0.2.0 window per §17.153 (4), and the baseline at `dee11301` is the base `bench compare` reads until then. Why: a release is the product at a point in time and a milestone gate is a verdict about one commit; the two coincide only by accident, and §17.238 (4) chose a pinned commit for the window precisely so that `main` could keep moving; a tag that waits for every push to settle never lands, and a freeze of hours is the cheapest way to get one green run on one SHA. Rejected: tagging `dee11301` (the alpha's version, no security row, no C archives); a release branch (one branch on the remote is the owner's standing rule); re-running the window on the candidate (the window is the gate's evidence, not the release's, and the owner has one night). Performance: none. Changed: `m4-exit-checklist.md`'s closing paragraph (this round). Impact: the owner (approve the candidate SHA; push the tag after one green run), every agent (hold pushes during the freeze), Sol (the preparation commit's checks).

251. **Deterministic counters are reportable anywhere: the WS-W1/W2 frame counts go back into the `0.1.0` changelog; the "no unblessed benchmark numbers" rule covers times, ratios, peak RSS and any other host-dependent measurement, not counts the emitted code fixes (changelog agent's question 5; §17.153, §17.191 (2), §17.199, §17.247; round 28).** Facts: the changelog agent dropped the `handled_*` (1,005 → 4 frames per `run(1000)`) and the callback-loop counts (1,121, 2,508, 5,010, 2,005 and 7,005 → 4) as a precaution; those numbers come from the module's `stats()` counters, recorded in `bench_counters.txt`, identical on every host and every run, and §17.199 (4) already lets a frames counter settle `countdown`'s bar; the same section keeps `restarts`, `reuse_attempts` and the "406 MB to 5.4 MB" file size, which are deterministic too; the rule's reason (§17.153) is that load on the shared machine moves timings, and a count of frames does not move under load. Decision: counts the compiler or the runtime fix deterministically (frames, restarts, reuse attempts and hits, candidates, module and file sizes, instruction and node counts, fixture tallies) may be quoted in the changelog, the notes, the landing page and the docs at any time, with the program, size and backend named; timings, Sakura/hand-JS ratios, peak RSS, compile latencies and anything else `bench run` samples stay out until a blessed window reads them, except in design entries and plans, which already mark advisory readings as advisory. The two WS-W1/W2 bullets return as written (Astra, with (248)'s changelog edit). Why: the rule protects claims from noise, and a counter has none. Rejected: keeping counts out to be safe (a true, repeatable fact withheld makes the changelog less useful to the agent reading it); a per-number approval (the rule is enough). Performance: none. Changed: nothing beyond the changelog. Impact: Astra.

252. **The reference machine stays the owner's M4 Pro for every window to 1.0; no cloud or VM window; nothing is cut from the window's protocol for `v0.2.0` or the rc without a noise study of the `--stable` configuration that does not exist; the one change made now is that a window resumes at the first suite that was not quiet instead of starting over, because each suite's file carries its own quiet verdict (owner's question through the changelog agent, question 6; §17.109, §17.110, §17.153, §17.175 (7), §17.238 (4); round 28).** Facts: the window is four runs, about 4–4.5 hours: `--suite js` and `--suite wasm` with `--stable` (2 s warm-up, a ≥ 30 ms batch, nine samples, five fresh processes per cell), `--suite native --lane matched` (the Rust, Go, OCaml and Koka controls under pinned toolchains) and `compile`; the warm-up is most of each cell's wall time; the baselines are keyed by host id (`bench/baselines/<host-id>.json`, `d88970189598`) and §17.109's ceilings were set on this host; the noise study in `bench/README.md` characterised the PR configuration (250 ms warm-up) and says it "does not establish the noise of the stable nightly configuration"; `record_load.py` reads the host's load average and its busiest executables, which on a shared-tenant VM cannot see steal time; §17.153 rejected a paid host and §17.175 (7) forbids emulated numbers; the owner's first window attempt failed for load, not for length; the procedure says "on `not quiet` keep the file, stop, and start the window again later", without saying whether a suite already completed quiet must be rerun. Decision: (1) **The reference machine stays** for `v0.1.0`, `v0.2.0` and the rc: a new host is a new host id with a baseline history of zero and ceilings that were never read on it, a shared VM's noise is invisible to the quiet verdict, and the window costs the owner a night the machine is idle, not hours of their day (§17.245 (4)). A faster window on another machine would be a different measurement, not the same one sooner. (2) **No cut without evidence.** `--processes` stays 5 (the RSS statistic and the confirmation groups are defined on five), the warm-up stays 2 s, every size runs, and no program is skipped as "unchanged": the window measures a commit's whole output against hand JS on one night, every cell shares that night's host state, and the result file records no per-program output hash from which "unchanged" could even be read. The evidence that would let a cut be decided is a noise study of the stable configuration on the reference host: two runs of one unchanged build in one quiet night at the current settings and one at the candidate settings (1 s warm-up, three processes), per-cell bands compared as the weekly `noise` job does; if the bands agree, §17.153's protocol can name the cheaper settings. That night is the owner's to offer, and it is not before the rc: a shorter window saves part of a night the owner sleeps through anyway, and a wrong number costs a release. (3) **Resumable window, now.** A suite's run is its own file with its own `meta.host.quiet`, blessed on its own; a window that aborts on a non-quiet run keeps every completed quiet run and resumes at the suite that was not quiet, the same night or the next, on the same commit in the same worktree; the pairing `envelope` reads (wasm file, native file) is already a pairing of two runs hours apart, so two nights are the same kind of pairing. `docs/release.md` §2's sentence reads "keep the file, stop, and resume at that run later; completed quiet runs stand" (Astra, one sentence; `run-window.sh` in the handoff brief gains a skip of a suite whose file is quiet, Sol, optional). Why: the quiet verdict is the thing that makes a run evidence, and it is per run; what the protocol forbids is rerunning a cell inside a run to get a better number, not keeping a run that was clean. Rejected: a cloud reference host (a different measurement, and a paid one); carrying the native controls forward from the previous window (their toolchains are pinned but the night is not); `--sizes quick` in a window (direction only). Performance: none; the window's length is unchanged until the study exists. Changed: `docs/release.md` §2 (one sentence, Astra). Impact: Astra, Sol (optional), the owner (a night for the study, if ever, after the rc).

253. **Three contract readings for the docs agent: `source_not_utf8` is `V0015` (`V0014` is `named_argument` and codes are never reused); `symbol_query 1.0` and `manifest 1.1` are stable from 0.2.0 as marked; `[permissions] process` is reserved: `process = []` is accepted and means what the absent key means, any other value is `V8006` until an RFC adds a `Process` effect (docs agent's questions 7–9; §17.232, §17.239 (c), §17.242 (2), (5c), §17.243 (3); round 28).** Facts: `codes.txt` has `V0014 active named_argument` and its header says every assignment is kept forever; §17.243 (3) assigned `V0014` to `source_not_utf8` without reading the file, and `docs/spec/diagnostic-codes.md`, `grammar.md`, `gaps.md` and the errors index copied the number; the next free `V00xx` is `V0015`; `symbol_query 1.0` and `manifest 1.1` are rows of `compiler/contracts/json.txt`, §17.242 (2) ruled `manifest` 1.1 right and (5c) made the MCP results the CLI's records by construction; `manifest.rs` declares `permissions.process: Vec<String>` ("Programs `Process` may start"), the startup denial maps an effect named `Process` to the `process` key, the design's §9 example writes `process = []  # no subprocesses`, and no `effect Process` exists in std or anywhere in the tree. Decision: (1) **`V0015 source_not_utf8`**; §17.243 (3) is read with `V0015`; Opus allocates it in `codes.rs` and `codes.txt` with the fixture, and Astra corrects the four documents in the same commit or the next. (2) **Confirmed**: `symbol_query 1.0` and `manifest 1.1` are stable from 0.2.0; the JSON split (§17.242 (1)) renames three summary kinds and touches neither. (3) **`process` is reserved**: the key stays in the manifest grammar, `process = []` parses and grants nothing (the same as leaving it out), and a non-empty list is `V8006` with the message "`process` grants nothing in this version: no std effect starts processes; the key is reserved"; STABILITY.md's `sakura.toml` rows gain the line (reserved; `[]` only; 0.2.0); a `Process` effect, when wanted, is an RFC that turns the list into a grant. Opus, with the `V8006` fixtures, before `v0.2.0`, not needed for 0.1.0. Why: a grant the runtime cannot honour is a lie an agent reading the manifest would believe; a key that nothing reads but whose empty form appears in the design's own example is cheaper to reserve than to refuse. Rejected: reusing `V0014` (the file's one rule); refusing the `process` key outright (invalidates the §9 example and the fixture for no gain); accepting a non-empty list silently (today's behaviour, and the lie). Performance: none. Changed: §17.243 (3) read with `V0015`; STABILITY.md (Astra); the four spec and docs files (Astra). Impact: Opus (`V0015`, `process` under `V8006`), Astra.

254. **Diagnostic and generated text is not a contract, so wording fixes land whenever they pass the gates; the four named ones land tonight in one Opus commit if CI is green on it before the preparation commit, else in the next version; user-facing text never names a milestone, a round, a plan or a version other than the compiler's own, and the `D096` text drops the environment name. Order after round 28 (docs agent's question 10; RFC 0001 "human wording… may improve", STABILITY.md's wording sentence; round 28).** Facts: `sakura_core/src/lower/mod.rs` says "`[permissions]` arrive in M3" in `V9002`'s text; `manifest.rs` builds `V8005`'s message from `CARGO_PKG_VERSION` as "Sakura {version}" (the brand rule is "Sakura Lang", never "Sakura" alone; the version is the compiler's own, not hard-coded); `D096`'s text in `codes.rs` names `SAKURA_MAX_HEAP`, which the JS and WASM hosts do not read (the module's memory maximum is fixed at build) and only the experimental native driver reads from the environment, so STABILITY.md's "this checkout does not read them" is right for the shipped backends and wrong for native; `compiler/examples/cookbook.md` says "pre-alpha APIs can change" and feeds the skill through `agent_docs`, whose mirror, ZIP and manifest must agree (`agent_docs --check` is a release gate, `docs/release.md` §3); RFC 0001 and STABILITY.md both say human wording and diagnostic prose are not contracts; the codes' identity and JSON fields are. Decision: (1) **Not a contract change.** A message's text may change in any version; what may not change is the code's condition, its `kind` and fields, and its class. (2) **Land tonight if green**: one Opus commit, `V9002` rewritten to what §6.2 and §9 say today (which effects the driver installs root handlers for and that `[permissions]` grants them), `V8005` as "Sakura Lang does not support packages yet: `[dependencies]` is reserved and refused; packages arrive in a later minor" (the RFC's MUST, no version), `D096` as "the WASM runtime's heap limit (ABI §13) was reached or memory could not grow", the cookbook's sentence as "pre-1.0: read STABILITY.md before depending on an API", the website error pages and the skill mirror regenerated, fixtures and snapshots updated and reviewed; the commit precedes the preparation commit only if its `ci.yml` run is green before the owner is ready to prepare; otherwise it waits for the freeze to lift and ships in 0.1.1 or 0.2.0. The tag never waits for a wording fix. (3) **The rule**: user-facing text (diagnostics, help, generated pages, the skill, templates) names no milestone, round, plan, agent or release other than the compiler's own version; a test asserting a message checks the sentence, so a stale sentence is a failing snapshot, not a contract event. (4) **STABILITY.md's runtime-limits row** reads "the JS and WASM hosts do not read these from the environment; the experimental native driver reads `SAKURA_MAX_HEAP`" (Astra). **Order after round 28**, ranked: **1** the window tonight on `dee11301` (the owner; `docs/release.md` §2; resumable per §17.252 (3)); **2** the release-flag change (Sol; §17.249 (2); `release.yml`, `release.py`, `docs/release.md` §6; dry run green on every row) and the docs edits before the tag (Astra; §17.248 (5), §17.251, §17.253 (1)'s documents, §17.254 (4)); **3** the wording commit (Opus; §17.254 (2)) if green in time; **4** bless, the gate signature, `release.py prepare`, the freeze, one green `ci.yml` run on the candidate, the tag, the three approvals, `verify-published.yml` on `0.1.0` (the owner, Sol runs the dispatch; §17.250); **5** after the tag: the per-row platform results on the install page (Astra; §17.248 (2)), `compat` and the ABI fixtures (Sol, Opus; §17.245 (5)), the Windows `autocrlf` case (Sol; §17.248 (4)), `V0015` and `process` under `V8006` (Opus; §17.253), then §17.246's list from its item 2 (`exec` first). Why: text that teaches an agent the wrong thing is a bug like any other and is fixed at the speed of the gates; a contract is what a program can parse, and no program parses a sentence. Rejected: holding the wording for 0.2.0 on principle (nothing protects a stale sentence); delaying the tag for it (the one thing that must not wait). Performance: none. Changed: STABILITY.md's limits row (Astra). Impact: Opus, Astra, Sol, the owner as ranked.

255. **The dogfood corpus under the owner's role rule: Claude Opus 5.5 writes all six programs, one fresh session each with no checkout of the repository; the second family's part is non-code by construction, the brief, the reader's review and the migration list, which GPT-6-Astra writes from the published docs and release notes alone; the cross-family writing evidence is the agent-DX eval's per-family numbers; the rc notes state the corpus as produced and never call it two-family (owner's role rule and two confirmations, 2026-10-19; §17.225 (2), (3), §17.245 (2), (3), §17.246 item 4; plan `road-to-1.0.md` stage 7; round 29).** Facts: the owner set a standing role rule today: Claude Opus 5.5 writes every line of code in the repository (compiler, runtime, CI, scripts, website); Claude Fable 5.1 decides design and writes no code; GPT-6-Astra and Fable research and may tell Opus what to do; GPT-6.1-Sol does simple non-code chores only; asked whether a GPT model may author a dogfood program, the owner answered that Astra can research and tell Opus what to do and that Sol is for simple tasks only. §17.225 (2) and §17.246 item 4 had three programs written by Claude agents and three by Codex agents, each from the installed binary, `sakura setup`'s skill and the website only, never from the compiler's source, and after `v0.2.0` an agent of the other family upgrading each program from the release notes alone; §17.225's reason was that two model families are the independent population that exists. No `dogfood/` directory exists, so nothing written is lost. §17.225 (3)'s agent-DX bar is already per family (final success ≥ 10/12 and pass@1 ≥ 8/12 in the skill condition, no task failing on both), the second family's run being the subscription episodes through the owner's Codex seat, judged by `runner.py judge` from a submission directory produced outside the runner. The two-family clause tested two separable things: that an author with no access to the compiler's source can write a real program from the published artifacts alone (the docs test), and that a reader of another make, with other reading habits, finds the docs and the notes sufficient (the second-reader test). A fresh Opus session knows no more about Sakura than a fresh Codex session, since nothing about this language is in either model's weights; what the source bar removes is context, so the docs test survives the rule whole as long as the writing session holds no checkout of the repository. What the rule removes is a second family writing 300 lines and 20 tests and meeting the language's friction at the keyboard. Decision: (1) **All six programs are written by Claude Opus 5.5**, one fresh session per program, with no checkout of the repository and no path to one, from the installed binary, `sakura setup`'s skill and the website only, as §17.225 (2) already requires of every author; the header records the author (`Claude Opus 5.5`), that the session was fresh, and the release built against; six sessions, not one, so no program borrows another's context. (2) **GPT-6-Astra holds the second family's part, which is non-code by construction.** Before Opus starts, Astra writes each program's brief as `dogfood/<program>/BRIEF.md` from the website alone: what the program does, the std surface it uses, the acceptance scenarios in prose, no code; every gap Astra hits is a dated `REQUESTS` or docs item. After the program lands, Astra reviews it against the docs as a reader, editing nothing, and files every friction it finds the same way. The friction items of both readers are the corpus's docs yield and each names its author. (3) **The upgrade keeps its cross-family test where it can keep one.** After `v0.2.0` tags, Astra writes `dogfood/<program>/MIGRATION.md` for each program from the release notes alone, before Opus touches the program: every change the notes require, each with the CHANGELOG line that explains it. Opus applies the list and nothing else. Acceptance is all six passing on 0.2.0 with every hunk of the diff on the list; a hunk Opus needed that the list did not name is a notes defect fixed before the rc, as §17.225 (2) already says of an unexplained break; a listed change the program did not need is recorded in the migration file. (4) **The cross-family writing evidence is the agent-DX eval's**, §17.225 (3) unchanged: twelve tasks per family in the skill condition, the Codex subscription episodes as the second family's run. The eval's submissions are judged in a submission directory and never enter the repository, so they are not code in the repository and the role rule does not reach them. **Owner question**: confirm this reading or overrule it. If Codex may not produce eval submissions either, 1.0 carries no cross-family evidence at all and the rc notes say the second family is untested; that is the owner's call to make, not one to let happen by omission. Recommendation: confirm. (5) **The rc notes state the evidence as produced**, in stage 7 (a)'s numbers: six programs written by Claude Opus 5.5 without the source, briefed, reviewed and migration-listed by GPT-6-Astra, the count of friction items by author, the migration lists' misses, and the eval's per-family numbers as the cross-family writing evidence; the phrase "two model families" is not used of the corpus. (6) **Conditional**: if the owner widens the rule for `dogfood/` in writing, §17.225 (2)'s three Claude and three Codex authors return unchanged, (2) and (3) narrow to Astra's part of the three Codex programs, and no other plan text moves. (7) **The role rule re-reads the standing assignments**: every queue row that writes code, a workflow, a script or a manifest is Opus's from today, which includes the Sol halves of §17.245 (1) and (5) and of §17.246 items 2, 3, 5, 10 and 11 (`fuzz.yml`'s campaign input and corpus artifacts, `check_history.py --full-tree` and the `contracts` job, the Intel `rust` schedule, `deprecations.toml` and `release.py prepare`'s checks, the `compat` job); Sol keeps what the rule leaves it: running workflows, reading results, the mechanical doc edits; Astra keeps research, notes and the spec prose; §17.246's ranking does not change, only its names, and the lead owns the renaming. (8) **Two confirmations recorded**: the owner confirmed §17.245 (2) on 2026-10-19 (native leaves the `v0.2.0` and 1.0 gates; the plan has said so since `1b51934c`), and the tokens pasted in chat were rotated on 2026-10-19 (the owner's statement; handoff §6's open item closes). Why: the owner's role rule is a role decision and binds; a requirement the rule cannot satisfy is rewritten to what the rule can show, and the notes say what was shown; the docs test is the half of the clause that produces the fixes, and a fresh session without the source keeps it whole; the second-reader test keeps its cheapest honest form in the brief, the review and the migration list; the writing test moves to the eval, which already measures it per family at task scale, and the notes say the scale. Rejected: asking for an exception on the corpus (the owner answered the direct question today; re-asking spends the owner's attention on a rule set hours earlier); dropping the second family from the corpus silently (the rc notes would claim what was not done); a GPT model writing the tests only (tests are code under the rule); Fable writing programs (design writes no code); one Opus session for all six (shared context makes six programs one); counting the brief as the second family's authorship (a brief is not a program and the notes will not say it is). Performance: none. Changed: plan `road-to-1.0.md` (the header paragraph, stage 7 (a), (b) and its exit criterion, the week-0 and G timeline rows); `compiler/REQUESTS.md` (one line). Impact: the owner (confirm (4); (6) only if wanted), the lead ((7)'s names), Opus (six programs, the migrations, the former Sol halves), Astra (briefs, reviews, migration lists, the notes), Sol (the handoff's §6 and §7 lines as a chore).

256. **§17.254 (3) reaches every page a user or an agent reads, hand-written or generated: milestone names leave the docs pages, the landing stages, `llms.txt`, `std/INDEX.md` and the skill, each replaced by the status it stood for; the roadmap page is the one place a milestone is named, and names it with its purpose; the CHANGELOG is history and exempt, `changes.mdx` is a status page and is not; the cookbook's `// milestone: M3` is a harness directive the example runner reads, kept in the source and stripped from the page and the skill with the rest of the directive header; one Opus commit under the owner's role rule, with a sweep check so the names do not return (lead's question, round 30; `c73a5751`; §17.254 (3), §17.255 (7); round 30).** Facts: §17.254 (3) listed diagnostics, help, generated pages, the skill and templates; `a91f4209` applied it to the compiler's text and the generated pages, and the diagram fix found the names still in hand-written prose. The sweep today: `tour/memory.mdx` carries a backend table whose "Milestone" column (M0 onward, M4, M5) says nothing its "Status" column does not; `tour/capabilities.mdx` line 224 says "the broader M3 gates and maintainer security review remain separate requirements" when M3 closed and the review was signed on 2026-10-18; `tour/concurrency.mdx` line 175 says "experimental native work (M5)"; `agents/index.mdx` suffixes each row's design citation with a milestone and says "milestones are defined in design §14.3"; `agents/verify.mdx` line 6 says "(milestone M4)" and line 116 links "the M4 plan"; `agents/cassettes.mdx` line 104 disclaims "all M3 exit gates"; `agents/typed-holes.mdx` line 117 cites "the M3 acceptance tests"; `changes.mdx` line 8 says "`v0.1.0` closes milestone M4 and is not tagged yet"; `index.mdx` line 91 says "the roadmap lists every milestone, M0 to M5"; `stdlib.mdx` is generated by `website/scripts/generate-stdlib.mjs` from `compiler/std/INDEX.md`, whose line 10 ("modules marked [M3] are the design §14.3 M3 surface; they run on the JS backend", stale since WASM runs them), the `[M3]` module markers, "Tags (M3)" and "the M3 modules" reach both the page and the skill's `references/stdlib.md` through `agent_docs`; `website/lib/source.ts` line 85 writes `llms.txt` with "the core language and M3 standard library on JavaScript"; the landing `roadmap.tsx` names a stage "M4 exit" and opens another's body with "M0 to M3:"; `pillars.tsx`'s "M4 Pro" is a laptop. The cookbook: every `compiler/examples/*/src/main.sak` opens with the fixture-format directive header of `compiler/REQUESTS.md` (`// milestone: M3`, `// mode:`, `// spec:`, `// args:`); `sakura_cli/tests/examples.rs` reads `milestone` and skips projects above `EXAMPLES_MILESTONE = 3`, as `ui.rs` and `semantics.rs` do for their suites through `common::skip_reason`; `agent_docs/src/cookbook.rs` requires the exact line `// milestone: M3` and `// mode: run|test` before it embeds the whole source, header included, in the eight `website/content/docs/cookbook/*.mdx` pages and in `skills/sakura/references/recipes.md`, which the ZIP, the manifest and the `public/skills` mirror copy; `check-doc-sweep.py` finds a cookbook fence's project through the fence's `project=` attribute and never reads the page's header; `agent_docs --check` is a release gate. The roadmap page defines the milestones by purpose with their state, and every milestone name on another page is a pointer into it that the reader cannot follow without knowing the plan. The design log, the plans, RFCs, ADRs, reviews, `REQUESTS.md`, the handoff and `compiler/examples/README.md`'s milestone column are the repository's working record and were never user-facing text. Decision: (1) **The rule's scope is the reader, not the author of the text.** User-facing text is anything a user or an agent reads to use the language: every page under `website/content/docs/`, the landing components, `llms.txt` and `lib/source.ts`, `docs/llms.txt`, `compiler/std/INDEX.md` as the source of two of them, the skill and its references, the cookbook pages, templates, help and diagnostics; whether a hand wrote it or a generator did changes who fixes it, not whether it is fixed. The repository's working record (the design log, plans, RFCs, ADRs, reviews, `REQUESTS.md`, handoffs, harness READMEs, fixture headers) keeps its names. A citation of a design section (`design §12.4`, `§17.88`) stays: it points into the published design, which the pages document; a milestone, round, plan, agent or stage name points into a schedule the reader does not have. (2) **Two exemptions.** The **roadmap** (`roadmap.mdx`) is the one page that may name a milestone, because it is where the name is defined, and it names each with its purpose and state as it does today; every other page links to the roadmap and says the status word. The **CHANGELOG** is history and exempt whole, including the unreleased `0.1.0` section's "close of milestone M4": a release note records what happened under the name it happened under, and a reader who meets the name there finds the roadmap one link away. `changes.mdx` is not history: it is a status page about `main`, and its sentence becomes "`v0.1.0` is the next release and is not tagged yet". (3) **Per item**, status words only ("complete", "experimental", "planned") or the fact the name stood for: `memory.mdx`'s table drops the "Milestone" column and keeps "the default; in every release", "complete; in every release", "experimental; source builds with the `native` feature only"; `capabilities.mdx` line 224 becomes "The escape rules, the cassette format and the template rule passed a maintainer security review; see the [roadmap](/docs/roadmap)"; `concurrency.mdx` line 175 "The experimental native backend targets single-thread execution"; `agents/index.mdx` keeps the design citation and drops the milestone from every row, and the sentence under the table becomes "The [roadmap](/docs/roadmap) says what is complete, experimental and planned"; `verify.mdx` line 6 drops "(milestone M4)", and line 116 reads "no release before 1.0; see the [completion plan](…)"; `cassettes.mdx` line 104 "All twelve examples execute in run or test mode; these three replay committed fixtures, which is not live-provider validation"; `typed-holes.mdx` line 117 "The compiler's acceptance tests require the language server, after replaying the same edits, to match `hole_context` byte for byte"; `index.mdx` line 91 "The [roadmap](/docs/roadmap) says what is complete, what is experimental and which releases lead to 1.0"; `std/INDEX.md` loses every `[M3]` marker, line 10 becomes "Every module runs on the JavaScript and WebAssembly backends", "Tags (M3)" becomes "Tags", "the M3 modules" becomes "every other std module", and `stdlib.mdx` and the skill's `references/stdlib.md` regenerate from it, with `stdlib.mdx` line 21 reading "`Sql.postgres` is not implemented and has no release assigned" and line 25 "Static verification is implemented for a restricted fragment; see the [roadmap](/docs/roadmap)"; `lib/source.ts`'s sentence becomes "The compiler runs the whole language and the standard library on JavaScript and WebAssembly, `sakura verify` proves contracts with Z3, and native code generation is experimental and in no release"; the landing `roadmap.tsx` stage "M4 exit" is named "WASM and verification" and the preview's body opens "The language, std, LSP, MCP, the skill, WASM and the verify preview, …"; `pillars.tsx`'s "M4 Pro" stays, it is a chip. (4) **The cookbook header is harness metadata and stays in the source; the page and the skill show the program without it.** `cookbook.rs` strips the leading directive lines (every line matching `// name: value` in the fixture format, and the blank line after them) from the source it embeds, and nothing else; the `sakura check`/`run`/`test` lines above the fence already carry the mode and the arguments. The directive header itself does not change: `examples.rs`, `ui.rs` and `semantics.rs` read it, the fixture format is the harness's, and §17.254 (3) does not reach a fixture. The eight pages, `references/recipes.md`, the ZIP, the manifest and the `public/skills` mirror regenerate in the same commit, so `agent_docs --check` stays green. (5) **A sweep check** so the names do not return: `check-doc-sweep.py` fails on `\bM[0-5]\b` or the word "milestone" in `website/content/docs/**/*.mdx` except `roadmap.mdx`, in `skills/sakura/**/*.md`, in `docs/llms.txt` and in the `llms.txt` text of `lib/source.ts`; the landing `.tsx` files are read by hand, since their SVG path data (`M2.5 6.3 …`) and "M4 Pro" would need an allow-list a regex does not deserve. (6) **Who and when**: Opus, one commit (§17.255 (7): website prose is website code), now; Astra reads the result as the reader and files any sentence that still teaches a schedule; Sol nothing. The commit is a wording commit under §17.254 (2)'s order: it precedes the preparation commit only if its `ci.yml` run is green before the owner is ready, else it waits for the freeze to lift. The tag never waits for it. Why: the rule's reason was that a sentence teaching the reader something they cannot use is a bug; a hand-written sentence teaches the same wrong thing as a generated one, and the diagram fix shows the names drift back where nothing checks. The roadmap is where a name earns its meaning, and history keeps its names because rewriting it would be the lie. The cookbook header is not prose; it is the harness's record of the program, and a program shown to an agent should be the program an agent would write. Rejected: reading (3) as generated text only (the reader does not know which pages were generated); rewording the CHANGELOG (history); renaming the roadmap's sections to status words (then nothing on the site defines the milestones the plans and the CHANGELOG use); keeping the cookbook header on the page with a note (a note explaining a harness directive is more text about the plan, not less); changing the directive to a status word (`// status: complete` would need every suite's skip rule to change for a header nobody reads on the page); a regex over the `.tsx` files (two false positives on day one); asking Astra to write the sentences (website prose is in the owner's Opus list; Astra reviews). Performance: none. Changed: nothing in this document beyond this entry; `compiler/REQUESTS.md` (one line). Impact: Opus (the commit: eleven pages, `INDEX.md`, `source.ts`, `roadmap.tsx`, `cookbook.rs`, `check-doc-sweep.py`, the regenerated outputs), Astra (the reader's pass), the lead (order: a wording commit under §17.254 (2)).
257. **The JSON baseline's one sanctioned rewrite under a live `contracts` job: `json.txt` gains a `baseline 0.2.0` line that both readers know, and the only transition `check_json.py` passes without comparing is "no line → `0.2.0`", spent by content once it is on `main`; `audit_summary` keeps `snapshot` required; `defect`'s `spans` children are listed; the regression file is the runner's record, one shape; Opus's STABILITY rows are ratified and a code row changes with its code; the changes page reads "after 0.1.0" (lead's round-32 questions; §17.232 (b), §17.242, §17.245 (5), §17.250 (3), §17.253 (2), §17.254 (3), §17.255 (7); `6706b01c`; round 32).** Facts: `6706b01c` (Codex, 2026-10-19, after §17.242 was written) wired the `contracts` job into `ci.yml`, required by `ci-required`: it runs `test_json.py`, then `check_history.py` and `check_json.py --base $BASE_SHA`, where `tools/ci/changes.py` sets the base to the pull request's base commit, or on a push to `main` to the head of the last successful push or scheduled `ci.yml` run on `main`; so if the run on the rewrite commit fails for any reason, the base stays before the rewrite and every later push compares across it again, which means any exception has to hold for every comparison whose base predates the rewrite, not for one commit. Opus's held branch (`fb02e7d1` the required → optional refusal, `a0dd5103` the split with `defect` and `regression`, `0f99551b` the docs) does §17.242 as decided; `check_json.py --base origin/main` on it reports 28 errors, fourteen on `summary 1.0` (six fields removed, eight optional → required) and fourteen on `summary 1.1` (removed), and the checker has no exception path; §17.242 (1) legalised the rewrite only by landing "before Sol wires the `contracts` job". `json_contracts.rs` reads `json.txt` too and panics on a line that is not five fields. `0.1.0` promises nothing of `--json` (CHANGELOG "No stability promise yet", §17.249 (1)); RFC 0001's promise begins at 0.2.0 if accepted; the file's header says "Append-only". `audit.rs` has always written `snapshot` in its closing record. Both backends give a defect's spans as `{uri, start_byte, end_byte, role}` (JS `violated` over the emitter's site table, WASM `defectSpans` over the debug section), no `content_hash`; `spans` is absent when there is no site (`D090`, `D096`, a trap). The runner sends the shrunk failure as `emit(JSON.parse(text))`, the CLI writes `serde_json::to_string_pretty` of that value to `tests/regressions/<function>.json` and drops the record from the `--json` stream; the old wire envelope `{kind: "regression", name, text}` was never baselined. `0f99551b` rewrote STABILITY.md's three JSON Lines rows and the MCP row to the code; §17.242 gave those rows to Astra; §17.255 (7) moved every code row to Opus and left Astra "research, notes and the spec prose" and Sol "the mechanical doc edits"; the gaps sentence under the table still says "doc/manifest need record identities", stale since `bcfe2166`, and the branch edits that sentence. `changes.mdx` on the branch reads "After 0.1.0, the closing summary records split into one kind per command"; `stability.mdx`'s "Changes planned before v0.2.0" loses the item; the CHANGELOG entry sits under `[Unreleased]`; §17.254 (3) forbids naming another release in user-facing text; §17.250 (3) freezes `main` from the preparation commit to the tag push. Decision: (1) **The reset is a line in the file, honoured once, by content.** `json.txt`'s first non-comment line becomes `baseline 0.2.0`, read "the history of this file is append-only from the release named here". Grammar: exactly one `baseline MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` line, before every field line; `check_json.py`'s `parse` returns it beside the entries; `json_contracts.rs`'s reader skips it (one line). `compare(previous, current)` reads the two lines first and there are six cases: (a) previous has no line and current's is `0.2.0`: **the reset**; no field line is compared, the script prints "JSON contract baseline reset to 0.2.0: N lines replace M" and exits 0; (b) neither has a line: today's rules unchanged, so `main` stays gated until the rewrite lands; (c) both have the same line: today's rules; (d) both have a line and they differ: "baseline changed from X to Y: the one reset is spent"; (e) previous has a line and current has none: "baseline line removed"; (f) previous has none and current names anything but `0.2.0`: "a reset names 0.2.0". Exactly once follows without the checker knowing any commit: the only passing transition is absent → `0.2.0`; once that is on `main` every later comparison has the line on both sides, (d) and (e) close the two ways back, and (b) and (c) are today's gate. It survives the base rule: however many pushes compare against a base that predates the line, each is case (a). **What the checker accepts**: (a), (b) and (c) under the additive rules as they stand (an added line with the next MINOR of its kind that keeps every earlier line as it was, a new kind at 1.0). **What it refuses**: (d), (e), (f), and under (b) and (c) everything it refuses today: a removed line, a changed type, optional → required, required → optional (`fb02e7d1`), a skipped MINOR, a MAJOR bump. **Tests** in `test_json.py`: one per case (a)–(f), a second `baseline` line and a malformed version as parse errors; the existing cases run under (b) and (c); `json_contracts.rs` is unchanged in what it checks. Across the reset the checker checks nothing else: the shapes stay honest because `json_contracts.rs` pins every line to real output in the same commit, and the reset diff is reviewed by the lead by name (AGENTS.md's named review for a semantics change). **Landing**: the line, the two readers and their tests join `a0dd5103` (one commit, so the commit that rewrites the file is the commit that says it may); `fb02e7d1` lands with it or before it (it changes the checker only and passes today); the branch stays held and lands as the first `main` commit after `v0.1.0` tags, so `0.1.0` ships the old shapes the freeze pins and the CHANGELOG entry stays under `[Unreleased]` as written. The README's `json.txt` paragraph states the line's meaning and that the reset is spent; RFC 0001's round-25 note under its unresolved questions gains one sentence (the baseline's history is append-only from the commit that writes `baseline 0.2.0`, before the tag); §17.242 (1)'s "before Sol wires the `contracts` job" is read as this entry. (2) **`snapshot` is required on `audit_summary`**, as listed. §17.242 (1) named the fields that distinguish audit's closing record from the others; `snapshot` is the identity field every closing record of a loaded program carries (`summary`, `verify_summary`), the emitter has always written it, and a field always written is listed required or the baseline under-promises for nothing. (3) **`defect`'s `spans` children are listed**: `spans[] object required`, `spans[].uri string required`, `spans[].start_byte integer required`, `spans[].end_byte integer required`, `spans[].role string required`; `spans` itself stays optional (no site, no array); no `content_hash`, since neither backend emits one (adding it is `defect 1.1`, later); the role values `primary` and `definition` are §12.2's and not a closed set in the baseline. The existing `run_defect` and `run_defect_wasm` cases pin the lines (their program violates a `requires`, so both spans are present). (4) **Yes.** The runner's `regression` record is the value on the runner's stdout and the file is the same value pretty-printed; whitespace and key order are not a contract (RFC 0001), so one kind covers both framings. The file is the contract surface, named by STABILITY's test row as Opus wrote it; the runner's stdout is the CLI's internal protocol (`runtime/js/ABI.md`), which the CLI consumes and does not forward, and if it is ever exposed it is the same record. A file without `kind` replays: a reader leniency within the compiler major (`kind` absent reads as `regression`; `schema_version` stays required), not a writer contract. (5) **Ratified, and the rule from here**: a STABILITY.md row that states what the code emits changes in the commit that changes the code, by that commit's author, so `main` never carries a row that contradicts its code; Astra keeps the prose and the first table's wording, reads every row change as the reader and files what misleads; §17.242's "Astra" for the rows is read so, under §17.255 (7). Two lines for `0f99551b` before it lands: the gaps sentence drops "doc/manifest need record identities" (stale since `bcfe2166`), and the Runtime JSON row says `defect` 1.0 with its spans listed, the same commit as (3). (6) **Confirmed.** On a page whose subject is 0.1.0, "after 0.1.0" names only the release the page is about and keeps §17.254 (3); "before v0.2.0" and the link to the planned-changes section go, as the branch does; `stability.mdx`'s planned list drops the item in the same commit. At the post-tag update the sentence moves into the 0.2.0 section of the changes page as a change, with the CHANGELOG entry it mirrors, and §17.256's "not tagged yet" line leaves then too. Why: a gate wired a day early is still the gate, and the one rewrite the design already owed is best recorded in the file the gate reads, so the repository's own history says when the promise began; a transition keyed on content holds under a base rule that may compare across the reset many times, where a commit range or a date would not; the additive route would keep a `summary 1.1` nobody emits that `json_contracts.rs` cannot check and a `summary 1.0` whose required fields cannot be stated without a bump; an agent reads a `defect` record to find the blamed call, and an open array promises it nothing; a row that lags its code is a wrong claim on `main` for as long as the lag lasts. Rejected: a version-boundary rule (removals allowed while the workspace version is below 0.2.0 or until the RFC is accepted: unguards `main` for the weeks to the tag and permits more than one rewrite); a commit range or SHA in the checker (unknown until the commit exists, changed by a rebase, and wrong under the base rule); landing the split as new kinds only with the old shapes deprecated (the two reasons above, and 0.1.0 owes the old shapes nothing); a `# baseline` directive inside a comment (a rule hidden in a comment, when the Rust reader's one-line skip is cheaper); lifting the hold to land before the tag (§17.250 (3)); `content_hash` on defect spans now (neither backend has it; an addition is a later MINOR); leaving `spans` open (the one reason the record carries them). Performance: none. Changed: `compiler/contracts/json.txt` (the `baseline` line, the five `defect` spans lines), `check_json.py`, `test_json.py`, `json_contracts.rs` (the skip), `contracts/README.md`, RFC 0001 (one sentence), STABILITY.md (the gaps sentence, the Runtime JSON row), all on the held branch; §17.242 (1) read with (1). Impact: Opus (the line, the two readers, the tests, the spans lines, the two STABILITY lines, on the held branch); the lead (reviews the reset diff by name; merges it first after the tag); Astra (reads the rows); Sol none.
