{Console}`, `confirm(msg) -> Bool`, `prompt(msg, default) -> Option<String>` as functions, and Opus built them so in `std/console`, over `Console.print` and `Console.read_line`, with `confirm` printing `message [y/N]` and `prompt` printing `message [default]` when there is one, `Console.scripted(lines)` a `{Test}` handler whose `read_line` answers from `lines` then `None`, and `Console.captured` unchanged (`read_line` is `None`); `ff66cded`: at a scope's end the JS runtime and `sakura_rt` took the first unjoined child whose outcome was not `ok`, so when a child failed after an earlier sibling, the failure cancelled that sibling, the scope met the `cancelled` outcome first and cancelled the whole task, the failure never reached a surrounding `try`, and `main` ended with a defect record without a code (exit 70); the fix skips `cancelled` outcomes in both runtimes (one condition each), which `runtime/js/ABI.md` and `rt`'s `fiber_done` group rule already stated; the fixture `scope_failure_after_cancelled_sibling` agrees on JS, WASM and native; no ABI, signature, JSON or diagnostic contract changes, and the snapshot diffs are the corpus report, the validator summary and the fixture's own print; the tag's gate is the owner's bless of the counted baseline, measured on `dee11301` in a clean worktree, so `main`'s bytes do not move it (§17.263 facts; §17.265); the owner is about to bless, and the tag follows (C, for the record). Decision: **(1) The dialogs as functions, endorsed.** A function over the two operations is served by every handler, including a user's `handler Console`, so 4b's breaking surface is `Clock` and `Task` only, and the dialogs need no operation, no ABI line and no `Console.host` change; `confirm`'s `[y/N]` suffix and `prompt`'s `[default]` suffix are the RFC's text now; `Console.scripted(lines)` is endorsed under the plan's acceptance clause (test-only, `{Test}` row). **(2) `ff66cded` lands on `main` now**, cherry-picked as its own `fix(runtime)` commit with its changelog line under `[Unreleased]` → Fixed; PR #5 rebases onto it and drops the commit. §17.263 (2) holds breaking changes and ABI bumps, and this is neither: it makes both runtimes match their own written rule, changes no contract text, and carries a three-backend fixture; the behaviour it replaces is a crash with an uncoded defect record that no program can rely on. It is a behaviour change in the task runtime, so this entry and the changelog line are the owner's review input; nothing waits for that review, and an objection before the tag is one revert. Rule for the record: a fix that brings a runtime to its own documented rule, with no contract text changed and a fixture on every backend, is a `fix` commit on `main` while the tag is pending; the owner reviews it by its changelog line. **(3) The bless and the tag proceed as §17.263 (2) and §17.265 state**; 0.1.0 carries phases 0, 1, 2, R and 7a (JS and native) and this fix, and the preparation commit's notes say which (§17.266 (1) for the WASM line). Why: the RFC's signatures were the decision, and the smaller breaking surface is the reason they were functions; a failure that a scope silently turns into an uncoded crash is the kind of bug 0.1.0 should not ship when the fix is two one-line conditions and a fixture. Performance: none; one extra comparison per unjoined child at a scope's end. Changed: RFC 0002 §2.8; `docs/plans/web-apis.md` §2, phase 4b. Impact: Opus (cherry-pick `ff66cded` to `main`; rebase #5), owner (review the fix by its changelog line; bless; tag), Sol (none).
268. **Phase 2 (`std/url`, `std/searchparams`) stands as built with one change: `with_path` on an opaque-path URL is `Err(UrlError(OpaquePath))`, not the URL unchanged; the password never serializes; a host that needs IDNA, ASCII `xn--` labels included, is `Idna` until punycode; `ftp` is special; the WPT fixture is generated from its table under a staleness test; the 896-tuple literal is WS-P19 in the performance push, after the tag (RFC 0002 §2.2; plan `web-apis.md` phase 2; §6.4; §17.263 (3); §17.265 (6); round 37, 2026-10-20, after `3481039f` landed).** Facts: `3481039f` is the URL Standard's basic parser in pure Sakura (special schemes with host parsing, IPv4 in every radix, IPv6, default ports, dot segments, the percent-encode sets; opaque hosts and paths otherwise), `Url.resolve`, `to_string`, `to_url`, `origin`, the `with_*` setters, `search`/`with_search`, and `std/searchparams` as an ordered multimap; `Url` and `Url.is_valid` are unchanged, so the `url"…"` template, `Request.url` and `Http.host()` accept what they accepted; 150 WPT cases (`urltestdata.json` at `c48d5874`, the selection rule in the header of `tests/vectors/url.jsonl`) agree on three backends and all 875 non-IDNA upstream cases agreed on JS during development; `UrlParts.password` is `Option<Secret<String>>` by RFC §2.2, and `to_string` returns a `String`, which `Show`, `Log.event` and cassettes carry, so the WHATWG serializer's `username:password@` cannot be written without `Secret.expose`; the standard's `origin` never carries credentials; `parse_host` returns `Err(Idna)` for a non-ASCII host and for any label starting `xn--`, because the standard's domain-to-ASCII decodes a punycode label and re-validates it, which no decoder here can do; `with_scheme`, `with_host`, `with_port` and `with_credentials` return `Result<UrlParts, UrlError>` where the standard's setters ignore invalid input silently, and `with_path` returns the value, unchanged for an opaque path (`is_opaque(p)`), where the standard's `pathname` setter is a no-op; `is_special` lists `ftp` with default port 21, as the standard does, and RFC §2.2 listed `http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, `file`; `Test.fixtures()` is the package's `tests/fixtures` directory for cassettes, which a single-file semantics fixture does not have, so `url_parse_whatwg.sak` and its `.stdout` are written by `semantics.rs`'s `url_vectors` from the table, which fails when they differ; during development a list literal of 896 tuples (the whole non-IDNA set) compiled to a 6 MB `main.wasm` that ran ten seconds, while the shipped fixture is 150 rows in 9.4 KB of source; `sakura_lir::image` already builds a static block for constant data (§17.229 (2)) and §17.236 recorded V8's optimising tier aborting past about 16,000 guarded rows. Decision: **(1) The password never serializes, endorsed.** `to_string`, `to_url` and `origin` omit it; a `Secret` enters a `String` only through `Secret.expose` under `@trust` (§6.4), and a serializer is not that place. Basic authentication goes in `Request.secret_headers`, which the host sends as the header and which the redirect loop drops cross-origin (§17.263 (4)); a password in a URL would escape both rules. `to_url(parse(s))` of a URL with a password is the URL without it; the doc comment says so and `url_credentials_are_secret.sak` pins it. The username stays (a `String` by RFC). `origin` is not a difference: the standard omits credentials there too. **(2) `Idna` for every host that needs IDNA, `xn--` labels included, endorsed.** Fail closed: passing a punycode label through would accept labels the standard rejects. Such hosts stay reachable through `Url` and `Http.host()`, which the parser does not touch; punycode is the additive change RFC §2.2 names, and when it lands `xn--` labels are decoded and re-validated, never passed through. **(3) Failable setters return `Result`, endorsed; `with_path` joins them.** The standard's silent ignore is the surprise RFC §Rejected uses forbids; which URL a setter receives is data (§17.263 (3)), so the answer is a typed error, not `requires`. `with_path(p, path)` becomes `Result<UrlParts, UrlError>` with `UrlReason` gaining `OpaquePath`; `with_query` and `with_fragment` keep returning the value, because they apply to every URL, opaque paths included. Opus lands it on `main` now (an additive module before the tag; no contract), with the `_rejects_opaque_path` case. **(4) `ftp` is special**, endorsed; RFC §2.2's list was short and is corrected (default port 21; `origin` is a tuple for `ftp` as for `http`). **(5) The generated fixture, endorsed, and the rule for it.** A fixture written from a vector table is committed like any fixture (the harness and parity run it unchanged), names its table and its generating test in its header, and the generating test is the staleness gate; the plan's `Test.fixtures()` sentence is struck. **(6) The 896-tuple literal is WS-P19.** Six megabytes for 896 rows is code per element, and ten seconds is not linear construction, so WS-P19 measures first: a generated program of n = 100, 300, 896 and 3,000 constant tuples, bytes of `main.wasm` and of the JS, and instructions per element on JS and WASM, to locate the superlinear term (constructor code per element instead of the static image; list growth by copy; the dispatch loop's input count of §17.236). Then the fix: a literal of constants is static data, and construction is linear. Acceptance: `main.wasm` within four times the literal's source text, and instructions linear in n (the 3,000-to-896 ratio within 10% of 3.35) on both backends. It follows WS-P18 in the push of §17.265 (6) and lands after the tag: a codegen change moves the preparation candidate's bytes, and nothing in 0.1.0 needs it (the shipped fixture is 150 rows and runs inside the gate). Why: `Secret` rules are not relaxed for a serializer; refusing what cannot be validated is the fail-closed reading every parser here takes; a no-op setter hides a bug from an agent as surely as a thrown exception would; a generated fixture with a staleness gate is deterministic and runs on every backend; a literal is the first thing an agent writes to carry a table, so its cost must be linear. Performance: (3) none; (6) is the lane item, its budget stated above. Changed: RFC 0002 §2.2; `docs/plans/web-apis.md` phase 2; `compiler/REQUESTS.md`. Impact: Opus (`with_path` → `Result` with `OpaquePath` on `main` now; WS-P19 after WS-P18 and the tag), owner (none), Sol (none).
269. **Phase 3 (`std/headers`, `std/blob`, `std/form`) stands as built: `get(h, "set-cookie")` is `None`, a header value is Fetch's byte sequence and no name is refused as a credential, `Blob.text` is strict UTF-8 while `parse_multipart`'s text parts substitute U+FFFD, `Form` is a transparent record, `encode_multipart` `requires is_boundary(b)`, and `boundary()` is `----SakuraFormBoundary` plus 96 random bits (RFC 0002 §2.3, §6; plan `web-apis.md` phase 3; §17.263 (2), (3); round 38, 2026-10-20, after `753d00fd` and `d506e2b1` landed).** Facts: the three modules are pure Sakura, green on JS, WASM and native, with `Request` and `Response` untouched; `HeaderError(name, reason)` with `HeaderReason = InvalidName | InvalidValue` never repeats the value, since a value may be a credential; `FormLimit = MaxParts | MaxBytes | MaxFieldBytes` and `FormReason = Limit(FormLimit) | ContentType | Malformed(offset)` stand where RFC §6 wrote `FormError(Limit)`; `is_boundary` is `pub` and `@total` (RFC 2046's character set and length) and `encode_multipart` `requires` it, so a bad boundary is `D020` like `Encoding.encode`'s `encodable`; `Form` is `{ entries: List<(String, Part)> }` with no `get`/`append`/`set`; `get(h, "set-cookie")` returns `None` where Fetch's `get` joins the values with `", "` (WPT `header-setcookie.any.js`), a join that is lossy because `Expires` holds a comma; a value is trimmed, then refused for NUL, CR, LF or any character above U+00FF (`InvalidValue`), which is Fetch's byte-sequence rule and what Node's `fetch` refuses, and a lookup or `remove` with a non-token name matches nothing; `Headers` holds no `Secret` by its type, and `Serve` delivers an incoming `authorization` in ordinary headers, so `Headers.of(req.headers)` must accept the name; `Blob.text` fails `Utf8Error` with the offset and drops a leading BOM where the File API substitutes U+FFFD; `parse_multipart` checks `max_bytes` against the input length before reading, then each part's count and content size, decodes a text part with U+FFFD as Fetch's `formData()` does, gives a part with `filename` the media type `text/plain` when `Content-Type` is absent (RFC 7578 §4.4) and `last_modified` the epoch (a pure function has no clock), reads back `%22`, `%0D`, `%0A` in names (the inverse of HTML's escape), ignores preamble and epilogue, and does not read `filename*` (RFC 7578 §4.2 forbids it); encoding follows HTML's algorithms and 56 WPT cases in `tests/vectors/form.jsonl` generate `form_encode_wpt`; `boundary()` is `----SakuraFormBoundary` followed by 16 Base64url characters, 96 bits of `Random`; `Blob.source` waits for `std/stream` and a binary file in an HTTP body for `Payload`, so `cookbook/form_upload` sends CSV; no ABI, JSON or diagnostic contract changed. Decision: **(1) The signatures are endorsed and enter RFC §2.3**: `HeaderReason`, `FormLimit`, `FormReason` (RFC §6's `FormError(Limit)` becomes `FormError(Limit(FormLimit))`), `is_boundary` with `encode_multipart`'s `requires`, and `Form` as the transparent record. The boundary is a program fact like the encoding in `Encoding.encode` (§17.263 (3)); `boundary()` always satisfies it, and a fixed test boundary is literal. No `get`/`append`/`set` on `Form`: `entries` is a list, list functions serve, and the `SearchParams` set would be a second multimap API for the same shape. **(2) `get(h, "set-cookie")` is `None`, endorsed; RFC §2.3 now says so.** The `", "` join corrupts a value that contains `Expires`, and a reader who wants the cookies calls `get_set_cookie`; returning `None` makes the mistake visible at the first test instead of at the first cookie with a date. **(3) The value rule and the no-credential-names rule, endorsed.** Fetch's byte sequence is the rule both ends of a request apply, so what `Headers` accepts is what the host sends; a character above U+00FF has no header encoding and is refused, not transcoded. `Headers` refuses no name: an incoming `authorization` is ordinary data on the server side, and the type already keeps a `Secret` out, so the outgoing rule (`Request.secret_headers`, §6.4) is a doc comment, not a validator. **(4) `Blob.text` strict, `parse_multipart` substituting, endorsed, with the rule.** A decode the caller asks for returns `Result` with the offset (`String.from_bytes`'s rule); a parser whose unit is the whole form substitutes in one text field as Fetch's `formData()` does, because rejecting the form for one byte in one field is the worse failure and would differ from every browser's reading of the same body. A caller who needs strict text sends the field as a file part and calls `Blob.text` on it. **(5) `parse_multipart`'s six choices, endorsed.** The length check before any read is the cheap fail-closed order; `text/plain` and no `filename*` are RFC 7578's words; the epoch for `last_modified` keeps the function pure, and a program that needs a time sets the field after `Clock.now()`. **(6) `boundary()`'s format, endorsed.** The fixed prefix makes a Sakura body recognisable in a capture, as `----WebKitFormBoundary` does; 96 random bits make a collision with part content negligible, and `encode_multipart` does not scan the parts for the boundary (a fixed boundary in a test is the caller's choice; the doc comment says so). Why: each reading is the fail-closed or the specification-literal one, and the one place Fetch is not followed (`set-cookie`) is where Fetch itself is lossy. Performance: none measured; `parse_multipart` on a 1 MiB body ran inside the std test's default budget (plan acceptance). Changed: RFC 0002 §2.3, §6, metadata, §Compatibility; `docs/plans/web-apis.md` §1, §2, phase 3; `compiler/REQUESTS.md` (the 2026-10-20 phase-3 entry answered). Impact: Opus (none on `main`; the doc comment on `encode_multipart` names the no-scan rule if it does not already), owner (none), Sol (none).

270. **The held series before and after the tag: PR #6's zeroing of every freed copy of a kind-`secret` import's arguments is split out and lands on `main` before the tag as a `fix(runtime)` commit with no import, export or version change; each held PR carries its own `test_bench.py` ABI assertion (PR #5 sets `0x010500`); phase 4a is built now as a held PR stacked on PR #6 at ABI 1.7.0, merged last (ABI §0, §8.1; §17.263 (2); §17.266 (1); §17.267 (2); round 38, 2026-10-20).** Facts: PR #6 (`hold/webapis-7a-wasm`, one commit `9779f4cf`, stacked on PR #5 `hold/webapis-4b`) adds the five `crypto_*` `hosted` imports at ABI 1.6.0 and, in the same commit, fixes a bug that ships in v0.1.0 otherwise: on the WASM host the three kind-`secret` imports (`http_send`, `http_stream_open`, `js_handler`, `sakura_rt::vt::SECRET_IMPORTS`) encode their arguments revealed through `vt_encode_tuple`, whose `StrBuf` grows by copying, so the blocks the growth abandons and the `String` that `string_to_bytes` copies from were freed with the secret still in them, and only the final transport `Bytes` was zeroed (`wasm.rs`'s `drop_transport`); ABI §8.1 already said "the guest zeroes the encoded transport `Bytes` before freeing it", which that sentence read as the whole encoding; the fix in `9779f4cf` is a `wipe` flag on `StrBuf` (`scratch.rs`: zero before `free` in `grow` and `strbuf_free`, and `finish_bytes`, which copies into a `Bytes` and zeroes the `String`), one line in `vt_encode_tuple` that sets it when `Sched::vt_secrets` is set, and the test `a_wipe_buffer_overwrites_every_block_it_leaves_behind`; the `rt_vt_begin`/`push`/`end` path never runs with `vt_secrets` set (a `Secret` there is redacted), so `vt_encode_tuple` is the one encoder of revealed secrets; the Node host's `decodeSecret` already zeroes its copied slice; the same commit's `Transport.wipe`, the `rt_vt_wipe` export, `rt_vt_result`'s fill, `top::BYTES`, `WASM_HOSTED` and the host's `wipe` entries serve the crypto imports and are 1.6.0; `bench/harness/test_bench.py` asserts `stats["abi_version"] == 0x010400` on `main`, PR #5 bumps `abi.rs` and the host to 1.5.0 without touching the assertion, so PR #5's CI fails on its own base and only PR #6 corrects it, to `0x010600`; PR #4 (`hold/json-split`) changes no ABI; phase 4a (plan) changes what `http_send` and `http_stream_open` carry in both directions (`Payload` bodies, `redirect: "manual"` on every send) and edits `sakura_runtime.js`, `sakura_wasm_host.js`, `std/http.sak` and `ABI.md`, the files PR #5 and PR #6 edit; §17.266 (1) set the merge order #5, #6, #4, then 4a, and ABI §0 forbids a skipped MINOR number. Decision: **(1) The zeroing fix lands on `main` now, split out of PR #6.** It is §17.267 (2)'s kind: it brings the guest to ABI §8.1's own sentence, changes no import, no export, no byte format and no version (checked: the hunks below touch none of `abi.rs`, the import table, `exports.rs` or the host), and carries a runtime test. Opus makes one `fix(runtime)` commit from these hunks of `9779f4cf` and nothing else: `compiler/runtime/rt/src/scratch.rs` (the `wipe` field and its doc, `StrBuf::wipe`, `wipe: false` in `strbuf`, the fill before `free` in the growth path, the fill in `strbuf_free`, `finish_bytes`); `compiler/runtime/rt/src/vt.rs` in `vt_encode_tuple` only (`if self.sched.vt_secrets { b.wipe(); }` and `Ok(()) => self.finish_bytes(b)`); `compiler/runtime/rt/tests/vt.rs` (the test, its comment citing this entry instead of 1.6.0); `compiler/runtime/rt/ABI.md` §8.1, the sentence extended "and every intermediate copy the encoder frees" with an erratum note in the file's style ("erratum 2026-10-20, design §17.270 (1): until then the blocks the encoder's growth abandoned and the `String` it copied from were freed unzeroed"), the version line untouched at 1.4.0; `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` → Security, one entry. Not in it: `Transport.wipe`, `rt_vt_wipe`, `rt_vt_end`'s and `rt_vt_result`'s changes, `top::BYTES`, `WASM_HOSTED`, the host's `wipe` option. PR #5 rebases onto the fix; PR #6 rebases onto PR #5 and its 1.6.0 line in ABI §0 drops the sentence "The same erratum applies to a kind-`secret` import's encoding…", which is now history under 1.4.0. The owner reviews it by its changelog line as security reviewer; nothing waits for that review (§17.267 (2)'s rule). **(2) Every held PR is green against its own base at every commit; PR #5 sets `test_bench.py` to `0x010500`.** Rule for the record: an ABI version bump is one commit that touches `abi.rs`, `sakura_wasm_host.js`'s `ABI_VERSION`, ABI.md §0 and `test_bench.py`'s assertion; a held PR whose CI is red on its own base is not mergeable, whatever the PR above it fixes. PR #6 keeps `0x010600`; PR #4 needs nothing (it rebases after both). **(3) Phase 4a is built now on `hold/webapis-7a-wasm`, as `hold/webapis-4a`, a PR against PR #6's branch, at ABI 1.7.0.** The host must read a `Payload` body in a request and `redirect` on every send, so ABI §8.2's `http_send` and `http_stream_open` lines change and §0 gains a MINOR entry; MINOR numbers are consecutive, so 1.7.0 exists only above 1.6.0, which fixes the base. The base is also the right one without the bump: 4a edits the three files that #5 and #6 edit, and a stack resolves those edits once, where a branch from `main` resolves them at the end against two merged PRs. Merge order after the tag stays #5, #6, #4, 4a; 4a rebases onto `main` after #4 merges (a small rebase; #4 is JSON). The PR carries `0x010700` in `test_bench.py` by (2) and the owner's review as security reviewer by §17.263 (4). If Opus finds the host needs no new §8.2 line (the answer already carries bytes and the request can carry a `Payload` as the existing kinds), the number stays 1.6.0 and the base is unchanged. Why: a secret left in freed guest memory is the kind of bug 0.1.0 does not ship when the fix is contained and tested; the held series is reviewable only if each layer is green and each ABI number has exactly one PR; a stack of three is one daily rebase chain, which is less work than three branches converging on the same host files. Performance: (1) one `fill` per abandoned block and per finished buffer of a kind-`secret` import only, three imports; nothing for the rest. Changed: RFC 0002 §Compatibility, metadata; `docs/plans/web-apis.md` §1, §2, phase 4a; `compiler/REQUESTS.md`. Impact: Opus (the `fix(runtime)` commit on `main` now; PR #5's `0x010500`; rebase #5 and #6; build 4a on #6), owner (review the fix by its changelog line; the tag follows unchanged), Sol (none).

271. **Phase 4a (`hold/webapis-4a`, PR #7, `1f7f0ea9`, ABI 1.7.0) stands as built, with two additions before it merges: `Request.bytes` and `Request.text`, and the PR's `REQUESTS.md` hunk dropped in favour of the entry on `main`; RFC §7's native startup refusal is its own row, built right after 4a merges (RFC 0002 §2.4, §7; plan `web-apis.md` phase 4a, row B; §17.263 (4); §17.270 (3); round 39, 2026-10-20).** Facts: PR #7 is one commit on PR #6's branch; `std/http` has one private `follow` (tail-recursive on the hop count) and `follow_stream` (closes a 3xx body before the next hop) that `host()`, `scoped()`, `scripted()` and `recording()` all call, each hop reaching the next handler with `redirect: Manual`, so a stack follows once in the first handler that receives the request and every inner handler sees one hop at a time; `next_hop` keeps phase 0's rules and messages (`7dd9dd47`'s `fetchFollowing`, now deleted): 301, 302, 303, 307, 308; `Error` fails `HttpError(Some(status), "unexpected redirect")` with or without a `location`; `Follow` returns a redirect with no `location` as it is (checked before the hop count, as Fetch does); the 21st redirect is `too many redirects` with no request sent; a location that does not parse or resolve is `invalid redirect location <location>`; a non-`http`/`https` location is `redirect to <scheme>: refused`; a hop whose `Url.origin` differs drops every `secret_headers` entry and any ordinary header named `authorization` or named like a `secret_headers` entry, for the rest of the chain; a 303 (not after `HEAD`) and a 301/302 after `POST` become a body-less `GET` without `content-type`, `-encoding`, `-language`, `-location`. `Http.host()`, `Serve.host()` and cassette replay deliver `Bytes` (`Empty` with no bytes); builders make `Text` or `Empty`; `Response.text` and `json` substitute U+FFFD, `Request.json` is strict (`BadRequest("body is not UTF-8")`). `Request.with_header` sets (earlier pairs of the name removed, any case) and does not validate; `with_headers(h)` replaces the list. A request body has no reader, so `sign_webhook` and `form_upload` `match` on `req.body`. Cassettes store a non-UTF-8 body as `body_base64` / `response_body_base64` and key on the body's bytes. ABI 1.7.0 changes no import name, vt tag or byte layout; what changes is the record `http_send`, `http_stream_open` and `serve_listen` carry (§8.2) and that the host no longer follows. Opus also migrated the eval task `07-health-route` to revision 3 (`.body` compared to `Text("v1")`, starter hashes recomputed), outside the brief. RFC §7's startup refusal (exit 75 for a native `main` whose row leaves `Http`, `Serve` or `Llm` to the runtime) is not built; native fails at first use with `D091`. Decision: **(1) One loop, four handlers, ratified.** The rule for the record: redirect following is a property of the `Http` handler that receives the program's request, never of the host; every hop is a separate request to the next handler with `redirect: Manual`, so a handler below sees exactly one hop, checks what it checks (`scoped` its list, the host `net`) and records what it records (`recording`: one exchange per hop); `Http.scripted` follows a scripted 3xx with a `location` as `host()` would, which is why the redirect cases are semantics fixtures on three backends and no longer runtime tests. **(2) Phase 0's rules and messages, ratified unchanged.** Fetch's HTTP-redirect fetch is the reference: redirect statuses, `Error` on any of them, `Follow` returning a `location`-less 3xx (the count is not consumed), the 21st hop failing, the body-less `GET` rewrite, the origin test on scheme, host and port. The dropped set stays `authorization` plus every `secret_headers` name, applied to `headers` too: `headers` carries no credential unless the author says so, and naming it in `secret_headers` is that statement; `cookie` and `proxy-authorization` are not added to the set (std sends neither; an author who sends one as a credential puts it in `secret_headers`, as `Request`'s doc says). **(3) A host body is `Bytes`, `Empty` with none, never `Text`, ratified**; the rule: a variant must be decidable from the request, never from the bytes' luck. `Response.text`/`json` substituting while `Request.json` is strict is the §17.269 (1) rule applied: a server answering a client's bytes fails the request (400) rather than reading a different document; a client reading a server's bytes follows `text()`. **(4) `with_header` sets without validating, ratified**: the RFC's example chains it without `try`, `with_headers(try Headers.of(…))` is the validating path, and the host refuses an invalid pair at send with `HttpError`. **(5) `Request.bytes` and `Request.text` are added in 4a.** `pub fn bytes(req: Request, limit: Int) -> Bytes ! {Fail<BadRequest>}` returns `Empty` as zero bytes, `Text(s)` as `String.to_bytes(s)`, `Bytes(b)` as `b`, failing `BadRequest { detail: "body exceeds {limit} bytes" }` past `limit`; `pub fn text(req: Request, limit: Int) -> String ! {Fail<BadRequest>}` is `bytes` decoded as strict UTF-8, failing `BadRequest { detail: "body is not UTF-8" }`, and `json` becomes `Json.decode(text(req, limit))`, so one reader holds the limit and the UTF-8 rule. Both are Fetch's `Request` readers; a server body reader is the common case (every webhook) and a five-line `match` in every recipe is the surprise. `sign_webhook` and `form_upload` use `Request.bytes`; RFC §2.4 names both. **(6) Cassette matching on the body's bytes, ratified**: `Text` and `Bytes` of one body are one exchange, and `body_base64` is the storage of a body that is not UTF-8, the BOM kept so bytes round-trip. **(7) ABI 1.7.0 MINOR, ratified.** The rule for the record: a change to the record a kind-`secret` import carries, with the transport's tags and layouts unchanged, is MINOR; §8.2's line is the contract the host reads, and the MINOR refusal (a 1.6 host refuses a 1.7 module) is exactly the protection wanted, since a 1.6 host would follow redirects itself and decode `body` as a string. **(8) The eval-task migration, ratified**: revision 3 of `07-health-route` with its starter hashes recomputed is the only way the task type-checks under `Payload`; a breaking phase migrates every in-repo consumer, eval tasks included, in its own commit, bumping the task's revision. **(9) The native startup refusal is row B of the plan, built by Opus right after 4a merges and before phase 5.** Scope: a native binary whose `main`'s effect row, after handling, leaves `Http`, `Serve` or `Llm` to the runtime exits 75 at startup with "`Http` is not available on target `native`" (one line, stderr, the effect named first), before any user code runs; `D091` stays for any other use; `WebSocket` joins the set in phase 8. A fixture that handles `Http` inside `main` (`Http.scripted`, every redirect case) is not refused, since its row is empty. Tests: one run-mode fixture under `compiler/tests/semantics` with a native-only expectation in `parity.rs`'s mechanism for declared differences, cited in the fixture header; JS and WASM unchanged. It is not a build-time diagnostic: the binary is built once and may run where the service exists later; no new diagnostic code. **PR #7 before merge (Opus)**: (a) `Request.bytes`, `Request.text`, `json` over `text`, a `test` block in `request.sak`, both recipes on `Request.bytes`, `INDEX.md`, the stdlib page and the skill regenerated, `CHANGELOG.md` `[Unreleased]` → Added one line; (b) drop the PR's `compiler/REQUESTS.md` hunk on the next rebase, since its question and this answer are on `main`; (c) `follow`'s doc comment and ABI §0's 1.7.0 entry cite §17.271 beside §17.263 (4). Nothing else changes; the owner's review as security reviewer (§17.263 (4)) is unchanged and nothing waits for it. Why: one loop in Sakura is the fix phase 0 could not finish (the host cannot see `scoped`'s list); Fetch's rules are the reference the recipes and the agents already know; a request reader belongs where every server needs it; an ABI number that refuses the old host is the point of the number. Performance: none beyond the PR's (one Sakura call per hop; `scripted` matches per hop). Changed: RFC 0002 §Metadata, §2.4, §7, §Compatibility; `docs/plans/web-apis.md` §1, §2 (4a, row B), phase 4a, row B; `compiler/REQUESTS.md`. Impact: Opus (the three PR #7 items; row B after the merge), owner (none new; the tag and the merge order stand), Sol (none).

272. **The counted compare after WS-P14: `handled_reentry` n = 1,000 is carried under a named cause with one bounded fix attempt in WS-P20; `shapes` n = 50,000 is a location-sensitive cell, not a regression, and the harness gains a same-location A/A recount for any blocked Node cell plus the artefact path in `meta`; `map_set`'s 6% is the same reading; `sieve`'s peak RSS gets §17.136's confirmation group (plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1; §17.264, §17.265 (5), (6); `7790603e`; round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: `compare` at `7790603e` against `baselines/d88970189598.json` (the `320c9980` bless) reads `blocked` on two Node cells. (1) `handled_reentry` n = 1,000 +16.6%, bisected to `list_at`'s flat branch (ABI §7), after which V8 no longer inlines `fromLeaves` into std's `range`; n = 10,000 and up are unchanged and the program is 0.70× hand JS at its largest size. (2) `shapes` n = 50,000 +29.1% with `calls` 16 in both files: the same emitted directory counts 454 M with the old runtime in the agent's worktree and 380–392 M with either runtime in copies elsewhere; the blessed cell (381 M, 1.777×) sits below its neighbours (n = 10,000 2.222×, n = 100,000 2.239×) and the new cell (2.295×) sits with them, so the blessed cell is the outlier; five processes agree to 0.3% at one path and differ 19% between paths under `--predictable` (fixed hash seed, one thread, GC heuristics off the clock). `meta` records commit, host, engines, flags, seed and `calls`, not the artefact's path or the cwd; the bless ran from `../sakura-counted` (`release.md` §2) and the agent's worktree is under `~/.t3/worktrees`. `map_set:int` and `map_set:string` flag +6% with identical counts on the old and new runtime; `sieve`'s Node peak RSS rises 89 → 147 MB at n = 200,000 from one group. Decision: **(1) `handled_reentry` is carried, named here.** A cell is carried this way only when bisection names a code-size or inlining cause, the next size is within the flag threshold and the row in `bench/deltas.md` says so; WS-P18's sweep re-reads every carry. WS-P20 (§17.274) makes one bounded attempt: a `list_at` whose cached path costs what it cost before WS-P14 (the flat read behind a helper reached only on a cache miss, or an equivalent shape), counted on `handled_reentry` n = 1,000 and `sieve` n = 200,000; it lands when the cell returns within the flag threshold and `sieve` moves under 2%, else the carry stands. **(2) `shapes` is `environment`, not blocking, and names a harness defect: a counted cell is also a function of the artefact's location.** Opus, in `bench/harness/bench.py` and `bench/README.md` before WS-P15's compare: (a) `meta.paths` records the realpath of the artefact root and the cwd; (b) `compare` re-counts every blocked Node cell as an A/A pair in the same session and location, the baseline commit's artefact (built once into `bench/target/baseline/<sha>/` from a detached worktree at `meta.commit`) and the head's, interleaved, at the file's `calls`; the verdict reads head over the baseline recount at the usual thresholds and the row prints blessed, recount and head; when the recount itself is off the blessed number by more than the flag threshold the row says `location`; (c) one time-boxed session on the cause: the same artefact and old runtime at paths of three lengths and through a symlink, n = 50,000, with the two hypotheses to confirm or drop, V8's identity-hash sequence shifting megamorphic stub-cache aliasing (`shapes`' `match` over three constructors and its `..it` updates are the polymorphic sites) or a GC-phase alias; the finding goes into `bench/README.md`'s methodology, and no flag joins the Node command line without it; (d) `release.md` §2 names the bless path, `../sakura-counted` beside the checkout, and a compare that gates a landing runs from a tree at that path or uses (b). **(3) `map_set`'s 6% is the same reading**: flagged, not blocking, covered by (b). **(4) `sieve`'s RSS** gets §17.136's second group of five at n = 200,000, run with WS-P20's counts; confirmed, it is accepted for 0.2.0 under this entry with its cause (a 1.6 MB array grown by copying is large-object garbage until a full collection) and re-read at WS-W7, where the flat layout is designed once for both heaps. Why: one anomalous blessed cell is not a reason to move the ground, and a recount reads through it; an A/A pair at the same location is the one comparison that cancels what the location adds; a small-size inlining boundary with the larger sizes unchanged is a bounded cost worth naming, not a block. Rejected: re-blessing the baseline; reading `shapes` as a WS-P14 regression (the A/A moved as much); copying artefacts to a fixed temporary path (as arbitrary as any other path, and it hides the sensitivity instead of measuring it). Changed: `performance-r1.md` §4.1. Impact: Opus (the harness items, before WS-P15's compare; the `list_at` attempt and the RSS group inside WS-P20).

273. **`nbody`'s bodies in place: a list-element ownership fact is in scope as WS-P21, after WS-P15 and WS-P20, with distinctness from live element locals proved by an identity test at run time, not by a range analysis (plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1; §17.149, §17.201 (3), §17.265 (6); round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: after WS-P14 (i) `advance$o` sets its list in place but rebuilds each body record; updating `bs[j]` in place measured −32% more by hand (817 M → about 555 M, about 4.9× hand JS). WS-P13b's field rule updates a record in place when the record local is owned; `at(bs, j)` is a borrow of an element, and a list owning its nodes says nothing about who else holds that element: a record may sit at two indices, or in a local read earlier (`b = at(bs, i)` is live through the inner loop over `j`). Decision: **(1) The fact.** An owned list local may also have *owned elements*: every element came in from a fresh origin (a `fresh` builtin, a literal, a call of a fresh def, an owned record update), established by the builder that made it (`List.map` and `List.range` with a callback whose summary is fresh, a literal of record literals; a new column of the builtin table, "elements fresh when the callback is fresh") and preserved by an owned `List.set` or `push` of a fresh value; lost by any other store into the list, by sharing the list, and by any element read whose local escapes (stored, captured, returned, passed to a non-borrowing call). A consuming summary records whether its owned entry assumes owned elements; it does so only when the def has an in-place element site; a caller that cannot prove the elements calls the plain entry and `--dump owned` says `elements`. No third twin. **(2) The site.** `set(bs, j, {..bj, …})` with `bj = at(bs, j)` updates the element in place when `bs` is owned with owned elements, the update consumes `bj` (dead after), and every other live element local of `bs` is distinct at run time: the emitter guards the in-place path with one identity test per such local (`bj !== b`), at most two, else no in-place, and the guard's other arm is today's allocation. **(3) The packet.** The soundness argument (the slot and `bj` are the only references to the element, the guard excludes the live locals, so the mutation is unobservable), a fixture placing one record at two indices (`List.of([r, r])`, `push(xs, at(xs, 0))`) where the fact is lost and the result equals the persistent one, a fixture where the guard fails (`i == j`), `--dump owned` printing the fact, and the differential eval run with the fact forced off. Exit: `nbody` down at least 25% on Node counts at n = 100,000 with no other Node cell flagged. Why: the largest remaining arm on `nbody` is this one; the fact is a column on the existing analysis; the identity test is one compare and replaces coupling `opt::ranges` to the ownership pass. Rejected: a general alias analysis; proving `j > i` statically; a mutable-record escape hatch in the language; uniqueness by type (a `List<Body>` may hold one record twice). Impact: Opus (WS-P21, after WS-P15 and WS-P20).

274. **Cold-path raising is allowed as WS-P20: a defect on a never-taken path is thrown inline as a `Defect` instance, preallocated when its message is static, with every observable unchanged; the `D011` conversion moves from the throw to the predicate's catch (ABI.md §5; §17.114, §17.115, §17.264 (5); round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: `$rt.add`, `sub`, `mul` and `list_get_expect` call `defect(code, message)` on their failing arm, which reads `contractDepth`, builds the message and the `Defect`, and throws; `spectral_norm` 754 M → 556 M by hand (−26%) when those calls become a `throw` of a preallocated value, and 185 M against hand JS's 168 M with the checks removed, which stays out (the checks are semantics). V8 keeps a call on a never-taken arm in optimized code at about 26 instructions an iteration; a `throw` costs nothing until taken. A defect's observable surface is its code, message, `spans`, the task outcome `{ kind: "defect", code, message }`, the `--json` `defect` record, the exit status and the stderr line; no JS stack is printed for a `Defect` (`asDefect` reads `.stack` only for a foreign error, which is `D090`). Decision: **(1) The thrown value is a `Defect` instance in every case**: the task boundary, the nested driver, `defect_catch` and cancellation stay as they are; no sentinel protocol, since a foreign object reaching `asDefect` becomes `D090`. **(2) Every observable is byte-identical**: code, message, spans, the JSON record, the exit status and stderr, pinned by every `expect-defect` fixture, `json_contracts.rs` and the regression file; no diagnostic contract changes. **(3) `D011` is the predicate's catch, not the throw's depth check**: a `requires`/`ensures`/`where` predicate that can defect is bracketed by a `try` whose catch rewraps a `Defect` as `D011`; `contractDepth`, `contract_enter` and `contract_exit` go, and the emitter's rule for dropping the bracket (ABI §5) is unchanged. **(4) The object.** A defect with a static message (`D001` "integer overflow", `D002`) is one frozen module-level instance thrown as is; a defect carrying a value (`D003`'s number, `D030`'s message) is `throw new $rt.Defect(code, msg)` inline; no shared mutable instance, and spans are never attached to a shared one. `$rt.defect` stays for std externals and the runtime's own cold code. **(5) Scope**: the JS backend only; the rt's raising is its own (WS-W5 reads the WASM contract path); ABI.md §5 reads "a defect is a thrown `Defect` instance; `$rt.defect` is one way to raise it", no version change. Exit: `spectral_norm` down at least 20% on Node counts at its largest size; `nbody`, `sieve`, `countdown`, `contracts_plain` read; no Node cell flagged; the `list_at` attempt and the RSS group of §17.272 ride in the same row. Why: a check is a compare and a branch, and the cost was the call behind the branch; keeping the class keeps every catch site; moving `D011` to the catch is what the bracket already means. Rejected: removing the checks; a non-`Defect` sentinel; lazy message rendering through mutable singletons (shared state across tasks). Impact: Opus (WS-P20, first in the lane).

275. **WS-P15, `Map<Int, _>` and `Set<Int>`: the insertion log stays and the index becomes a persistent radix trie on the key's own bits, chosen at the first insert, with the `Map.get`-then-`unwrap_or` fusion as a second arm; insertion order, persistence after sharing and SameValueZero are the contract (plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1; §13.4, §17.116, §17.149, §17.217, §17.265 (6); round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: the runtime map is an insertion log (a `List` of `[k, v]` entries, `HOLE` on removal, compaction when holes outnumber entries) and a hash array mapped trie from `hashOf(keyOf(k))` to the entry's position, with `HLeaf`, `HNode` and `HColl` classes, `splice` into dense child arrays and owned entries writing in place. `run_int` at n = 100,000 on Node: the build 291 M (about 2,900 instructions an insert, owned), then `let snapshot = mi` shares the map and every later operation is persistent: 200,000 gets 129 M (`Option.unwrap_or(Map.get(…))` allocates a `Some`), 50,000 updates 202 M (a copied log path, the closure, a `Some`), 33,000 removes 105 M, iteration 82 M; 845 M against hand JS's 135 M with a JS `Map` and one copy for the snapshot. `K: Hash` excludes `Float`, so a key that is a JS safe integer is an `Int`, and one map holds one `K`. Copy-once-then-in-place measured +21%; dropping `splice` moved nothing. Decision: **(1) The contract**: insertion order (§13.4), SameValueZero on `keyOf`, persistence after sharing, the same `Show` and JSON, identical on three backends; unchanged. **(2) The index.** A map or set whose first key's `keyOf` is a safe integer takes an *integer index*: a persistent radix trie on the key's bits, five a level from the low end, branch nodes as `HNode` (bitmap, dense children), the bottom level one 32-slot array of positions indexed by `key & 31` (−1 absent); no hash, no `HLeaf`, no `HColl`; the root's level grows with the largest key, and negative keys live in a second trie on `-k - 1`. Every safe integer is a key, pinned by a fixture with 0, −1, ±(2^53 − 1), 2^31 and 2^32 ± 1. `K` is static, so every later key is an integer; Opus confirms no `keyOf` of another `K` yields a number, else the integer index rebuilds as a hash trie on the first other key (one `typeof` an insert). **(3) Owned and persistent paths**: the owned entries write the path in place as today; the persistent ones copy the branch nodes on the path and the 32-slot leaf, and the log path as today; update of an existing key touches the log only, as now. **(4) Fusion**: `Map.get` consumed at once by `unwrap_or`, `is_some` or `expect` becomes one builtin without a `Some` (`map_get_or`, extending §17.151's `map_get_expect`), for every key kind. **(5) Protocol**: WS-P13a's, the runtime hand-edited into the arms (the index without leaf objects, positions at the leaf, the fusion), each counted, a bucket landing only when it moves at least 10%. Exit: `map_set:int` down at least 35% on Node counts at n = 100,000, the Bun row read; `map_set`, `map_set:string` and `map_set:tuple` not regressed; the 3.0 ceiling is read at WS-P18. Why: the hash adds nothing for a key that is already a bounded integer, the leaf objects and the `splice` are the per-insert cost, and the log is the ordering contract. Rejected: a JS `Map` index (a remove after `snapshot` would copy it whole); a dense array (§17.217: dense ids are `List`; a `Map` may not assume density); a type-directed `map_empty_int` in the emitter (generic std helpers would miss it, and the first key decides at run time with the same result); copy-once-then-in-place (measured). Impact: Opus (WS-P15, after WS-P20).

276. **WS-P14 closes as landed; its two open arms are the rows WS-P20 and WS-P21; the JS lane's order is WS-P20, WS-P15, WS-P21, WS-P16, WS-P17, WS-P18, with WS-P19 in WS-P18's sweep (plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1; §17.265 (6); §17.268; `7790603e`; round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: arm (i) landed as the ownership rule (§17.278), arm (ii) landed for `List<Bool>` and measured against for `Float`/`Int` (−5% on `spectral_norm`, a flat read misses the leaf cache) and for references (+23% on `rbtree`, V8's collector); typed arrays need an element type the backend does not have at run time; arm (iii) measured −7%, under the bar; `spectral_norm` is unmoved by any arm. At the largest size on Node: `nbody` 7.23×, `sieve` 3.08×, `spectral_norm` 4.49× against the 1.3 ceiling. Decision: WS-P14 is done; the Float/Int flat list is closed on this backend and re-read only in WS-W7, where the WASM layout has a static element type; the record-in-place arm is WS-P21 (§17.273) and the cold-path arm is WS-P20 (§17.274); the three misses are named here. Order: WS-P20 first (smallest, and every checked loop in the suite gains), WS-P15, WS-P21, then WS-P16–WS-P18 as §17.265 (6) wrote them, WS-P19 (§17.268) inside WS-P18's sweep. Wave 2's trigger, "after WS-P14–WS-P16 land", now reads after WS-P16; the web-APIs start condition is §17.279. Why: a row ends when its arms are measured, not when its ceiling is met; the misses are findings with named next rows. Impact: Opus.

277. **Row B stands as built: the `secrets` example is the refused fixture, the stderr line stays one unprefixed line naming the first effect in sorted order, the unreachable `Llm` entry stays, and the "`D090` or `D091`" sentence is replaced by the code a native run shows (plan `web-apis.md` row B; RFC 0002 §7; §17.271 (9); `796e553e`; round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: a run-mode fixture under `tests/semantics` has no `sakura.toml`, so `sakura run` denies a `main` declaring `Http` on every backend before the program starts (design §6.2); the `secrets` example has a manifest with `net`, and carries `expect-exit@native: 75` and `expect-stderr@native` in its header; the negative case is `native_coverage_handled_http_runs.sak`; `sakura_host_native`'s driver test holds the line and the code; the line has no `error:` prefix; `Llm` in `main`'s row is `V9002` at build (no parameterless `Llm.host()`); `changes.mdx` and `roadmap.mdx` say a self-installed handler stops with "`D090` or `D091`", the driver's comment says `D091` at first use, and the native host's defaults answer `D091`. Decision: **(1)** The example is the fixture: it is the one program in the tree that may declare `Http` with a grant, and a fixture that reaches the driver needs one; no manifest fixture mechanism is added for this. **(2)** The line stays as built: it is the program's stderr, not the CLI's, so it takes no `error:` prefix; one effect in sorted order is one deterministic line. **(3)** The `Llm` entry stays, one line, for the day a host handler exists. **(4)** Opus runs a native binary that installs `Http.host()` and one that installs `Serve.host()` and records the code each stops with in the native CLI parity note; the two pages then name that code only, and phase 8's acceptance line already assumes `D091`. Impact: Opus (item 4, a short task before phase 5), Sol (the two pages after it).

278. **The WS-P14 ownership rule in `owned.rs` is ratified: a def with a fresh result consumes a parameter when owning it owns more update sites than the plain entry; the review the owner delegated is recorded here, with one precision follow-up (CODEOWNERS; §17.149, §17.201 (3), §17.265 (6); `7790603e`; round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: the change is twenty lines: `summarize` no longer returns `false` for every parameter of a fresh def; it runs the same `Analysis::run(…, &[p])` as for any consuming def and keeps `p` only when `a.owned_sites() > base.owned_sites()`, `a.owned[p]` and every return is owned, `parts = weak(&a)` as before. At a call, the result's origin is `Fresh` whenever the callee's summary is fresh (the plain entry still returns `List.map`'s list), and the argument at the consumed position is `Use::Consume`; a consume that is not the local's final use makes it `BorrowedAfter`, so the plain entry is called. `owned_updates.txt` changed by two lines and `owned_fresh_result` pins `advance$o` on both ABIs and WASM. Decision: **sound, ratified.** The owned entry of a fresh-and-consuming def is produced by the mechanism WS-P13b ratified, under the same caller obligation (owned, dead after the call); the new condition only decides whether a twin exists, and a wrong choice costs a copy, never a shared node. **One precision caveat, named**: a caller that keeps using the argument after the call now sees a non-final consume where it saw a borrow, and may lose its own later in-place sites on that local. Opus adds a fixture of that shape (the argument used after the call, then updated in place) with `--dump owned` pinned; if a site is lost, the call-site rule is refined so that an argument live after a call at the consumed position of a def whose plain entry borrows it is a `Borrow` (the plain entry is what runs). Impact: Opus (the fixture, inside WS-P20's commit).

279. **WebSockets and the rest of Bun's web APIs are being built (RFC 0002); the remaining phases run in the order 5, 9, 8, 6, 10, 7b, 11, 7c with 12 beside each, and the pure-Sakura phases 5 and 9 start now beside the perf lane instead of after WS-P16 (plan `web-apis.md` §2; RFC 0002 §2.5, §2.9, §7; §17.262, §17.263 (2), §17.265 (6); round 40, 2026-10-20).** Facts: the owner asked whether WebSockets and the whole Bun web standard library are being done. RFC 0002 and §17.262 committed every API on Bun's page in Sakura's shape; phases 0–4b and 7a are on `main` or merged after the tag, 7a-W as well; the WebSocket client is phase 8 (effect `WebSocket`, `connect`/`send`/`receive`/`close`, `scripted`, `net` grants, the native refusal joined); a WebSocket server (`Serve` upgrade) is outside the RFC and the page, a follow-up to `std/serve`. §17.265 (6) started phases 5–11 after WS-P14–WS-P16 land. Phases 5 (`std/stream`, pure Sakura plus `http.sak`/`fs.sak` adapters) and 9 (`std/urlpattern`, pure Sakura) touch no file the perf lane edits; phase 8 edits `sakura_runtime.js`'s scheduler, `sakura_wasm_host.js`, `validate.rs` and ABI.md, the runtime file WS-P20 and WS-P15 edit; 6 and 10 edit the scheduler and `rt`. Decision: **(1) Yes**: everything on the page ships before the rc, the WebSocket client in phase 8; the server upgrade is not promised. **(2) Order**: 5, 9, 8, 6, 10, 7b, 11 (two sessions), 7c last and optional; 12 with each phase. **(3) Parallelism**: 5 and 9 start now in the web lane's worktree beside WS-P20 and WS-P15; 8 starts when WS-P20 is on `main` and rebases over WS-P15 (its runtime edits are one new section and the scheduler's wait queue); 6 and 10 follow 8 in order; both lanes keep §17.263 (2)'s rule that neither waits for the other. Why: the two pure phases cost the perf lane nothing and 5 unblocks 8 and 6; the runtime file is the one shared resource, so the row that edits it least goes first. Rejected: holding 5 and 9 until WS-P16; starting 8 beside WS-P20 (two agents in one runtime section). Changed: `web-apis.md` §2 (an order paragraph), `performance-r1.md` §4.1. Impact: Opus (both lanes), Sol (phase 12 pages as each lands).

280. **A stream is a value: `Source<T, e>` is an unfold, `pull` returns `Done` or `Next(item, rest)`, a pure source is persistent and re-pullable, and a source over a resource is a view that lives where the resource lives; no runtime cell, no private cursor effect; `buffer` and `tee` move to phase 10 over `Channel`, codec-backed sources are callback-shaped views, and the RFC's `Limit` type and `Source.close`/`Sink.abort` go (RFC 0002 §2.5 amended; supersedes the `std/stream` parenthesis of §17.262 (2); §8.1, §8.4, §6.3; plan `web-apis.md` phases 5, 6, 10; `17d3b20d`; round 41, 2026-10-20).** Facts: Opus stopped phase 5 before any code (`17d3b20d`): RFC §2.5's `Source<T, e> = { pull: fn() -> Option<T> ! e, close }` is a record of closures, a closure captures by value and cannot assign an outer `var` (`V2041`, §8.1) or reach handler state (each `with` holds its own instance, §5.5), so a `pull` written in Sakura is a pure function of what it captured: `from_list` cannot advance, `take` cannot count, `lines` and `chunks` cannot keep a remainder, `tee` and `buffer` have no queue; checked against the compiler (`V2041` on a `from_list` that assigns its index). The only sources that advance today are the host-backed ones, `Fs.read_chunk` on a `File` and `Http.read_chunk` on a `Body`, where the position is the resource's, and both are scope-bound resources (§8.4; `Http.stream`'s callback, `Fs.with_file`'s callback). §8.1 names handler `var` state and `Graph` as the only stateful constructs, both confined; `Decoder.new/push/finish` (phase 1) already threads an immutable state and returns the next state with each result; `Channel.with(capacity, body)` (RFC §2.9, phase 10) is a bounded queue whose `Sender`/`Receiver` are scoped. Opus's options: (A) a runtime cell behind a scoped external (an ABI MINOR, a third stateful construct, §8.1 changes); (B) scoped sources, every stateful combinator a callback installing a private cursor handler whose operation appears in the source's row; (C) value-shaped sources, `pull` returning the item and the next source. RFC §1's example already composes `Http.body_source`, `Compress.gunzip_source`, `Encoding.decode_source`, `Stream.lines` and `Stream.fold`. Decision: **(1) (C), with the resource rule for the rest.** `std/stream` declares `pub type Step<T, e> = Done | Next(T, Source<T, e>)` and `pub type Source<T, e> = { pull: fn() -> Step<T, e> ! e }`: pulling a source performs its row and returns either the end or one item with the source that continues after it. A source has no `close`: a pure source holds nothing, and a source over a resource is closed by the callback that owns the resource. `pub type Sink<T, e> = { write: fn(T) -> Sink<T, e> ! e, close: fn() -> Unit ! e }`; `abort` goes, since a failure travels in the row. **(2) Two kinds, named in the docs.** A **pure source** closes over values only; it is persistent: pulling the same source value twice returns the same `Step`, so using one source in two places reads the same items from the same place (`tee` of a pure source is using it twice), and `Done` is stable. A **view** closes over a resource (`Body`, `File`; later a `Receiver` or a codec state): pulling it advances the resource, `rest` is an equivalent view, two uses of one view interleave on the resource (deterministically, one instance on one thread, §17.171), and it is scoped by §6.3's rule for a closure that captured a scoped value, so it cannot leave the callback that introduced the resource (`V6003`). An empty `Bytes` item from a pure source is data; the two host views end at the first empty chunk, as `read_body` reads today. **(3) Signatures (phase 5, all pure Sakura).** `pub error StreamError(reason: StreamReason)`, `pub type StreamReason = MaxItems | MaxLine`. `empty<T, e>() -> Source<T, e>`; `from_list<T, e>(xs: List<T>) -> Source<T, e>`; `map<A, B, e>(src: Source<A, e>, f: fn(A) -> B ! e) -> Source<B, e>`; `filter<T, e>(src: Source<T, e>, keep: fn(T) -> Bool ! e) -> Source<T, e>`; `take<T, e>(src: Source<T, e>, n: Int) -> Source<T, e>` `requires n >= 0`; `fold<T, A, e>(src: Source<T, e>, init: A, f: fn(A, T) -> A ! e) -> A ! e`; `each<T, e>(src: Source<T, e>, f: fn(T) -> Unit ! e) -> Unit ! e`; `to_list<T, e>(src: Source<T, e>, max_items: Int) -> List<T> ! {Fail<StreamError> | e}` (the item after `max_items` fails `MaxItems`, as `Response.bytes(r, limit)` fails its limit); `chunks<e>(src: Source<Bytes, e>, size: Int) -> Source<Bytes, e>` `requires size > 0` (re-chunks to exactly `size`, the last shorter, holding at most `size` bytes); `lines<e>(src: Source<String, e>, max_line: Int) -> Source<String, {Fail<StreamError> | e}>` (split on LF, a trailing CR removed, a final unterminated line yielded, a pending line past `max_line` by `String.len` fails `MaxLine`); `pipe<T, e>(src: Source<T, e>, sink: Sink<T, e>) -> Unit ! e` (writes each item, then `close`). In `std/encoding`: `decode_source<e>(src: Source<Bytes, e>, enc: Encoding, errors: Errors) -> Source<String, {Fail<EncodingError> | e}>` over `Decoder.push`/`finish` (an empty decoded chunk is skipped, `finish` runs at `Done`) and `encode_source<e>(src: Source<String, e>, enc: Encoding) -> Source<Bytes, e>` `requires encodable(enc)`. Views: `Http.body_source(body: Body, chunk: Int) -> Source<Bytes, {Http}>`, `Fs.file_source(file: File, chunk: Int) -> Source<Bytes, {Fs}>`, `Fs.file_sink(file: File) -> Sink<Bytes, {Fs}>` (rows as the operations declare them; `chunk > 0` required), and phase 3's `Blob.source(b: Blob, chunk: Int) -> Source<Bytes, e>`, pure. No `Limit` type, no `buffer`, no `tee` in phase 5. **(4) What later phases inherit.** Phase 10 builds `buffer<T, R, e>(src: Source<T, e>, capacity: Int, body: fn(Source<T, {Task | e}>) -> R ! {Task | e}) -> R ! {Task | e}` (a producer fiber pulls `src` into a `Channel` of `capacity` items and waits when it is full; the body's source is a view over the `Receiver`) and `tee<T, R, e>(src: Source<T, e>, max_lag: Int, body: fn(Source<T, {Task | e}>, Source<T, {Task | e}>) -> R ! {Task | e}) -> R ! {Task | e}` (two channels of `max_lag`); a byte bound is `chunks` before `buffer`, so `ByteLengthQueuingStrategy` becomes a gap row and `Limit` is not declared. Phase 6 keeps the whole-buffer functions and makes its streaming forms views over a scoped codec state, callback-shaped like the host views, `decompress_source<T, e>(src: Source<Bytes, e>, format: Format, max_out: Int, body: fn(Source<Bytes, {Fail<CompressionError> | e}>) -> T ! e) -> T ! e` and `compress_source` likewise; a codec state is mutable in both runtimes, so it is never a pure source. Phase 8's `receive` stays an operation; a socket source, if one is wanted, is a view. **(5) Acceptance for Opus (phase 5).** `stream_pull_persistent.sak` (one pure source pulled twice from the same value yields the same items; `Done` twice), `stream_from_list_take_map_filter_fold.sak`, `stream_chunks_bytes.sak` (an empty `Bytes` item from `from_list` is data; `chunks` re-sizes across item boundaries), `stream_lines_split_across_chunks.sak` (a line split across two items, CRLF, a final unterminated line), `stream_lines_rejects_max_line.sak`, `stream_to_list_rejects_max_items.sak`, `encoding_decode_source_split_sequence.sak` (a multi-byte sequence split across chunks), `stream_pipe_to_file_sink.sak` (`Fs.memory`), `http_body_source_scripted.sak`, `blob_source.sak`, `stream_view_cannot_escape.sak` (UI, `V6003`: a `body_source` returned from `Http.stream`'s callback; if the escape check does not reach a closure's captured resource today, that is a `design-question`, not something to work around), and the `V2041` reading as a comment in the module header (why a source is a value). Fixtures green on three backends with identical traces; `.wasm.stdout` for none; no combinator holds more than its argument names, reviewed by reading the module; the stdlib page, `INDEX.md` graph (`stream → list, bytes, string`; `encoding → stream`), the skill, `llms.txt`, `cookbook/stream_lines.mdx` and the `tour/memory.mdx` paragraph (a source is a value; a view is a resource's position) regenerated or written; the changelog names the module. No ABI, JSON or diagnostic change. Why: §8.1's value semantics is the whole reason a Sakura stream cannot be a JS stream; (C) is that rule applied, with `List` and `Decoder` as its precedents, and it makes a source an ordinary value an agent can hold, re-read and test without a scope; (A) would add a reference cell to a language whose memory model (§8.2) depends on their absence; (B) would make every list-backed stream a callback and put a private effect in every row; the places where a position really is shared, a resource or a queue, already have the scoped-callback shape (§8.4, `Channel.with`), and `tee`/`buffer` are queues, so they belong with the queue. Performance: a record and a closure per item, nothing per byte; byte sources are chunked at the caller's size, so the per-item cost is amortized over the chunk; no benchmark program streams, so no cell moves. Rejected: (A); (B); keeping `Source.close` (nothing to close on a value; a resource's callback closes it); `Option<(T, Source)>` instead of `Step` (a `match` on `Done`/`Next` reads better than a nested tuple and leaves room for nothing else, which is the point); a `Limit` sum type for `buffer` (one capacity in items, bytes bounded by `chunks`); yielding `Result` items from `lines` or `decode_source` (a failure travels in the row, like every other reader). Changed: RFC 0002 §1 (the stream rows), §2.5, §2.6 (one sentence), §6 (two rows), §8 (one phrase), its example; `web-apis.md` phases 5, 6, 10 and §2; §8.4 receives its sentence in phase 12. Impact: Opus (phase 5 now; phase 9 is done, so phase 8 follows as §17.279 ordered; phases 6 and 10 as written here), Sol (phase 12 items).

281. **Phase 9 (`std/urlpattern`, `b2fde35d`) stands as built: `PatternReason = Unsupported(String) | Duplicate(String) | Limit`, `UrlMatch { groups }` as the only match surface and `Request.params` the router's, `*` one segment and `**` zero or more (greedy, by table), segment-level syntax with every reserved character outside the subset `Unsupported`, empty segments ignored, raw values, literal origins through `Url.parse`, a route whose pattern does not compile `D020`, the two limits; the two divergences from the standard are gap rows; one doc-comment follow-up (RFC 0002 §2.2 amended; plan `web-apis.md` phase 9, §5; §17.262 (2), §17.269, §17.279; round 41, 2026-10-20).** Facts: the REQUESTS entry of `b2fde35d` lists six readings; `compile` is 242 lines of Sakura, `Router.route`/`get`/`post`/`put`/`delete` declare `requires UrlPattern.compile(pattern).is_ok()` and compile again in the body, whose `Err` arm returns the router unchanged and is unreachable under the contract; `handle` matches with `exec` and sets `params` from `groups`; every existing router fixture and example is byte-identical; the standard's `*` is `.*` and crosses `/`, and the standard is exact about a trailing slash; the plan's phase 9 named `*` and `**` as "available to routes" without fixing their meaning, and §5 left open whether `Router` exposes `UrlMatch`. Decision: **(1) Every reading is ratified** and is now RFC §2.2 text: `PatternError(reason: PatternReason)` with `Unsupported(text)` (the text that used the syntax), `Duplicate(name)` and `Limit`; `UrlMatch = { groups: List<(String, String)> }` in pattern order, unnamed groups `"0"`, `"1"`, … as the standard numbers them, no per-component `input`, no `test` (a keyword; `exec(p, url).is_some()` is the test); `*` is exactly one segment and `**` zero or more, greedy, its value the segments joined with `/` and `""` for none; a `:name` is a whole segment whose name is an ASCII identifier; a `:`, `*`, `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `?`, `+`, `#` or `\` anywhere else in a segment is `Unsupported(segment)`, never a literal, so a later release can give it the standard's meaning additively; empty segments are ignored on both sides (`/users/7/` matches `/users/:id`, as `Router` matched before); the query and fragment are never read; values are the raw segment text; a full-URL pattern is `scheme://authority/path` with a literal origin normalized and compared through `Url.parse` (lowercased host, default port dropped), and a relative `Url` never matches one; a pattern starting with `/` or without `://` reads `Url.path`; 4,096 bytes and 64 groups are `Limit`. **(2) `D020` for a route stands, double compile included.** A route is part of the program, like `encode_multipart`'s boundary (§17.269); the second compile runs once per route at construction, which is not a served path; the unreachable `Err` arm stays because the checker wants the match total. Follow-up, in the next commit that touches `router.sak`: the doc comment of `route` says that the reason is read by calling `UrlPattern.compile(pattern)` in a test, since a `D020` names the predicate, not `PatternReason`. **(3) Plan §5's question is closed: `Router` does not expose `UrlMatch`**; `Request.params` and `Request.param` are the surface, wildcards included (`Request.param(req, "0")`). **(4) Two gap rows for phase 12**, on the stdlib page and in the module header: `*` is one segment where the standard's `*` is `.*`, and a trailing slash is ignored where the standard is exact; each names the Sakura form and the reason (the router's existing contract; a meaning that can widen later without breaking a route). **(5) `bind`'s table** ((m + 1) × (n + 1) `Bool`s per request) is accepted; a linear walk for a pattern without `**` may land at any time as a `perf` commit with the fixtures unchanged, and nothing waits for it. Why: the readings keep every existing route byte-identical, refuse rather than reinterpret anything outside the subset, and give `Router` and `UrlPattern` one matcher; the one standard-visible divergence that matters, `*`, is forced by the RFC naming both wildcards and is cheaper to document than to make `*` cross segments in a router. Rejected: `*` as the standard's `.*` (then `**` is redundant and `/files/*` matches a whole tree, which no route author expects); exact trailing slashes (breaks `Router`'s contract); percent-decoding values (the standard's `exec` returns the input; decoding is the handler's, with `Url` functions); a `Result` from `Router.route` (a route is a program fact; `D020` is what the agent sees at the first request of a test, with the pattern text in the span). Changed: RFC 0002 §2.2 (the `UrlPattern` bullet), §Metadata (implementation status); `web-apis.md` §2 (row 9 landed), §5. Impact: Opus (the doc-comment line with the next `router.sak` change; nothing else), Sol (the two gap rows and the inventory row in phase 12).

282. **A fixed young generation joins the counted Node command line: `--min-semi-space-size` and `--max-semi-space-size` set to one value beside `--predictable`, for every Node process the harness measures on every OS, and a file records its Node flags so `compare` never reads two flag sets as one; the size is 16 MB if one bounded measurement reads the two locations within 0.5%, else the measured 64; the flag commit carries a candidate counted run, the owner re-blesses the `js` and `wasm` baselines at that commit, and WS-P20 and WS-P15 compare against whichever file `main` has when they compare, the old one through the A/A recount (`bench/README.md` "Location and the A/A recount"; §17.264, §17.265 (4), §17.272 (2), §17.136; `0216e570`; round 41, 2026-10-20).** Facts: §17.272 (2)(c)'s cause session found the location sensitivity of a counted Node cell to be a GC-phase alias: `shapes` n = 50,000 counts 481 M in the repository's `bench/target` and 391 M under `/tmp` with the same artefact and runtime, the identity-hash hypothesis is dropped (`--hash-seed` moves one place and not the other), and with the young generation fixed at 64 MB the two places count 373.7 M and 373.2 M (0.13% apart) and the WS-P14 recount pair reads +0.4% where the default reads +8.2%; `handled_reentry`'s +12.5% is unmoved by the flags (code, carried under §17.272 (1)); `--trace-gc` shows the same 32 scavenges and 3 mark-compacts at both places with the last scavenge differing in heap size and pooled pages. Under the default configuration a drift under the 5% flag threshold biases a row without being seen, and the recount runs only for a blocked cell and costs a baseline artefact per compare. `--predictable` is already on the counted Node command line (§17.264 (2)); `meta.flags` records `processes`, `suite`, `metric`, `seed`, not V8's flags; the blessed files `bench/baselines/d88970189598.json` and `wasm/d88970189598.json` are the `320c9980` runs that gated `v0.1.0`, which is published; peak RSS is gated by §17.136 as a head-over-base crossing, and a 64 MB semi-space raises every Node process's peak by up to the new space's size; V8's default maximum semi-space on 64-bit is 16 MB, grown from 1 MB; WS-P20 is next in the lane and WS-P15 after it, neither on `main`; agents may make counted runs and only the owner blesses (`release.md` §2); the candidate directory `bench/baselines/candidate/` exists for an unblessed run. Decision: **(1) Yes, the flag joins.** The counted Node command line is `node --predictable --min-semi-space-size=S --max-semi-space-size=S …` for every measured Node process, the `js` and `wasm` suites and the timed `--stable` runs alike, on macOS and on Linux CI, so a timed file and a counted file describe one engine configuration; Bun and Wasmtime are unchanged. **(2) `S`.** Opus measures `S = 16` first, `shapes` n = 50,000 and `binary_trees` at its largest size, five pairs an arm at the two locations of the cause session; 16 is taken when both cells read the two locations within 0.5% and the recount pair within the flag threshold, since it pins the young generation at V8's own ceiling and keeps peak RSS nearest a user's run; otherwise `S = 64`, the measured value. The session is time-boxed to the one measurement; the number and its readings go into `bench/README.md`'s methodology. **(3) Flags are recorded and never mixed.** `meta.flags.node` is the list of V8 flags the run used; a file without it is read as `["--predictable"]`; `compare`, `envelope` and `bless` refuse to read two files whose `meta.flags.node` differ, printing both lists, with a `flags` status in place of a number; `test_bench.py` asserts the command line and the refusal. **(4) The flag commit** (Opus, `bench/harness/bench.py`, `test_bench.py`, `bench/README.md`, `release.md` §2) lands on `main` as soon as it is green, before WS-P20's compare if it is ready first, and carries a candidate counted run of the `js` and `wasm` suites at that commit from `../sakura-counted` under `bench/baselines/candidate/`, with its `.md` tables under `bench/results/`. **(5) Owner step: re-bless at the flag commit.** The owner runs `release.md` §2 at the flag commit (or blesses the candidate files if their oracles are green and their trees were clean; `bless` already checks both) for the `js` and `wasm` suites; the `320c9980` files move to `bench/baselines/archive/320c9980/` with their flags, kept as evidence (`bench/README.md`'s rule); the checklist line names the new `meta.commit` and the flags. Until then, a compare against the candidate is direction and is marked `pending owner bless` in `bench/deltas.md`. **(6) Rows in flight.** WS-P20 and WS-P15 compare against the baseline file on `main` at the time of their compare: the blessed `320c9980` file through the A/A recount (`0216e570`), or the re-blessed file once it exists; a row that compares against the old file also runs the compare against the candidate and records both, and its exit criterion (§17.274, §17.275) is read on the blessed file. No row waits for the bless; the bless never waits for a row. `sieve`'s RSS confirmation group (§17.272 (4)) runs under the flags its baseline has. **(7) Nothing else moves**: thresholds (§17.110), §17.136's RSS reading, the same-engine ceilings (both sides of a ratio run under the same flags), the two envelope lanes (§17.265 (2)) and the `v0.2.0` gate's reading (a blessed counted baseline, §17.264 (1)). Why: the harness measures the compiler, and a count that moves 8–19% with the directory it runs from measures the directory; the flag removes a measured cause at no cost to what a ratio means, since both sides of every ratio run under it; the recount stays as the answer to any location sensitivity the flag does not remove, and the recorded flag list is what keeps the two eras from being read as one. Rejected: leaving the flag out and relying on the recount alone (a drift under the threshold is never recounted); a per-program flag (fitted to the cell it was found on); copying artefacts to a fixed path (§17.272 (2)); re-blessing without the flag (moves the ground and keeps the defect); holding the flag until WS-P15 lands (two more rows counted under a known defect, when the fix and the bless touch no file they edit). Performance: none in the compiler; every Node count changes once, at the re-bless, and only the ratios are read. Changed: `bench/README.md` (one paragraph), `performance-r1.md` §4.1 (one paragraph); `release.md` §2 with the flag commit. Impact: Opus (the flag commit: (2), (3), (4)), the owner ((5), one re-bless, about an hour of runs that agents may make), Opus in WS-P20/WS-P15 ((6)).

283. **WS-P15 is accepted as landed and closed; the three confirmed Node peak-RSS crossings of its counted compare are a harness defect, not a regression: a counted compare's RSS gate read the many-call processes, whose call count the head's own speed doubles and whose peak V8's collection phase sets, while the one-call processes already recorded in both files read lower on every crossed cell; the gate reads the one-call peak from here, with no re-measurement and no re-bless; `Map.update`'s second lookup is an arm of WS-P18's sweep, not a row (plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1; `bench/deltas.md` row WS-P15; `bench/results/2026-10-20-d88970189598-wsp15-ab.txt`; §17.136, §17.264, §17.272 (4), §17.275, §17.282; `5ac80fe3`, `5b545a04`, `f266098d`; round 41, 2026-10-20).** Facts: WS-P15's exit is met, `map_set:int` 839.7 M → 522.5 M (−37.8%) on Node counts at n = 100,000, `map_set` −16.4%, `map_set:string` and `map_set:tuple` within 1% at one location; the compare is `blocked` on three Node peak-RSS crossings confirmed by §17.136's second group, no count blocked. The counted run (§17.264) measures each cell as five pairs of a one-call process and a 1 + k-call process, k calibrated per file so the extra calls retire 2^32 instructions, and `rss_bytes` is the many-call process's peak; a faster head therefore calls more (`map_set:int` 8 → 16, `map_set` 16 → 32), and `bench/README.md` already says a short cell's many-call peak grows with its call count (the runtime keeps four objects of every finished task). At equal k, `map_set:int` reads 264 → 264 MB. `map_set` n = 10,000 (187 → 268 MB at k = 32) and `map_set:string` n = 50,000 (223 → 291 MB at k = 16) are moved by the `map_get_or` fusion alone (head without it 223 MB; head runtime on base's emitted code 223 MB): `--trace-gc` shows fewer scavenges, two mark-compacts instead of three, the first mid-call with more live data, the last at a larger heap (157–183 MB against 104–125) and a *lower* post-GC heap (22.4 against 29.2 MB; 16.4 against 22.5 MB): nothing is retained; with no `Some` per get the young generation fills later and V8's old-generation limit grows from a different phase, the GC-phase class §17.282 names. With a 16 MB fixed semi-space (the flag commit's first candidate) string reads 195 → 240 MB and `map_set` 197 → 168 MB. Both files carry every process's counters: the one-call peaks are `map_set:int` 121 → 98 MB, `map_set` 73 → 72 MB, `map_set:string` 84 → 80 MB, each stable to 1 MB over the five pairs. The flag commit (§17.282) is not on `main`; `bench.py` line 458 still adds `--predictable` alone. `Map.update` is std Sakura, `insert(m, k, f(get(m, k)))`: the update bucket counts 162.9 M of 522 M at n = 100,000 (50,000 updates, about 3,260 an update), of which two index walks are a minority beside the persistent log path, the closure and the `Some` that `f` takes. Decision: **(1) Accept.** WS-P15 stands as landed: the integer index and the fusion stay; nothing is carried, since no cell regressed in what the gate exists to catch (live memory). WS-P15 is closed; WS-P21 (§17.273) is next in the lane's order (§17.276). **(2) The defect, named.** In a counted compare the peak-RSS reading must not depend on a call count that the head's instruction count sets: comparing a 16-call process with an 8-call one is not a head-over-base reading of the program, and a faster head is punished by construction. The one-call process is the program run once, its peak is what a user's run pays, it is already measured on both sides at every cell, and it is the stable statistic (1 MB over five pairs where the many-call peak moves 40–80 MB with the collector's phase). **(3) The rule.** When every file of a compare is an `--instructions` run, the §17.110/§17.136 peak-RSS gate reads the maximum over the pairs' one-call `process_counters[*].one.rss_bytes` on both sides; the `rss` row prints the one-call maxima, the many-call maxima and `calls` of both files, and the confirmation group of §17.136 is read on the one-call maximum. The many-call peak stays recorded and printed as a diagnostic; it is never read by a verdict. Timed (non-counted) runs are unchanged: their processes run equal calibrated batches on both sides. Baselines are unchanged: the blessed `320c9980` files already hold the one-call counters, so no re-measurement, no re-bless and no `meta` change; the flag commit's re-bless (§17.282 (5)) proceeds as written. **(4) The fusion's reading is methodology.** The equal-k and `--trace-gc` readings of the `ab.txt` go into `bench/README.md`'s peak-RSS section as the second named GC-phase case after `shapes` (§17.282): fewer young allocations can raise a many-call peak while lowering the live heap, which is why the many-call peak is not a verdict. **(5) `sieve` n = 200,000 (§17.272 (4), 89 → 147 MB)** is re-read under rule (3) inside WS-P20 from the files already on hand; if its one-call peak crosses 25%, §17.272 (4)'s acceptance with its cause stands as written; if not, the row says so and the carry is dropped. **(6) `Map.update` is not a row.** A `map_update` builtin that walks the index once and writes the log at the position it found is the shape; by §17.275 (5)'s bar it lands only when hand-counted at 10% or more of its program, and the two walks are well under that at n = 100,000 on the integer index. It is a named arm of WS-P18's sweep (§17.265 (6)), counted there with the ceiling read; a `Some` per update stays, since `f` takes an `Option`.
