289. **The WebSocket server is in RFC 0002 and in 1.0: a served request is upgraded by `WebSocket.accept(req, options, body)`, an operation of the `WebSocket` effect whose socket is the client's `Socket` with the same `send`, `receive` and `close`, `Message`, `Received` and `CloseInfo`; the handshake is a pure `handshake(req)` shared by `host()` and `scripted`; `origins` is a list that refuses every browser origin it does not name; no extension, server frames unmasked and an unmasked client frame 1002; one socket limit for both roles, `SAKURA_MAX_SOCKETS`; Bun's topics as `subscribe`, `unsubscribe` and `publish(topic, message, except)` in the host, instance-local, a publisher never waiting; no idle timer and no pings sent; a refused upgrade is the handler's `Response` written by the host on the raw connection; the handler's return after an upgrade is discarded; phase **8s**, pre-rc, in the 1.0 contract, starting now in its own lane or after phase 6 in the web lane, before 10, at the first free MINOR of 8s and 10 by §17.266 (1); 7c in its own lane (owner's request, 2026-10-21; RFC 0002 §Non-goals, §1, §2.10 new, §4, §5, §6, §Security, §Tests, §Metadata amended; plan `web-apis.md` §2, phase 8s new, §4, §5; §17.279 (1), §17.285, §17.286 (4), (7), (10), (12), §17.288 (10); round 43, 2026-10-21).** Facts: the owner asked for the WebSocket server, "full parity with Bun including `Bun.serve`'s websocket support"; §17.279 (1) had said the server upgrade "is not promised" and RFC 0002's non-goals list `Bun.serve` upgrade hooks and "a WebSocket server (`Serve` upgrade): not on the page; a follow-up to `std/serve`". `Bun.serve`'s websocket offers `server.upgrade(req, { data, headers })`, the `open`/`message`/`close`/`drain` callbacks, `ws.send`/`close`/`ping`/`pong`/`cork`, `ws.subscribe`/`unsubscribe`/`isSubscribed`/`publish` and `server.publish` (topics), `maxPayloadLength` 16 MiB, `backpressureLimit` 16 MiB with `closeOnBackpressureLimit` false (a message past the limit is dropped, the socket kept), `idleTimeout` 120 s, `sendPings` true, `perMessageDeflate` false. Sakura's `Serve.serve(handle: fn(Request) -> Response ! e, addr)` runs each request as its own task under the handlers of the `listen` site (`runTask(handle, [value], ctx.h)`; `ctx.t` is the task; the WASM host keys served requests by task in `served`, and `serve_respond(task, …)` names the answer); `serveHttp` is `node:http`'s `createServer` with no `upgrade` listener, so Node routes an upgrade request to the `request` event with a `ServerResponse` that cannot hand its socket over; the WASM host's `served` map holds the reply closure per task. Phase 8's runtime (§17.286 (6), (7)) parses RFC 6455 in the client role: `wsData` fails a masked frame with 1002 (a server must not mask), `wsFrame` masks every frame, a socket is an `Int` in `files` closed by `file_closing`, `wsFull` holds the peer back at 64 messages or `max_message` bytes, a pong only while writable, `WS_CLOSE_MS` 5 s, 1001 on every exit of the callback. `Socket` is `@resource opaque` in `std/websocket`, constructed only there; `Request` and `Response` are pure records and a `Response` cannot carry a closure; a resource cannot leave its callback or be assigned to handler state (`V6003`, §17.260 (G06)), so a program cannot hold a list of open sockets, and fan-out to every connected peer cannot be written in Sakura from the operations phase 8 has. `std/websocket` is pre-rc and in no release (`6b633a99` after `v0.1.0`), so an operation added to `WebSocket` breaks nothing shipped; `Serve` is in 0.1.0 and an operation added to it is a 0.2.0 change for every user `handler Serve`. `WebSocket` and `Serve` are both in the native driver's `UNAVAILABLE` set (RFC §7, row B). ABI 1.9.0 is 7b-W, in flight; §17.288 (10) named phase 10 for 1.10.0; phase 6 is not on `main`. RFC §2.3 says `Serve` delivers `authorization` as an ordinary header: a credential's policy is the handler's. Node 22+ has a global `WebSocket` client, an implementation that is not ours, usable as the runtime test's peer; `SAKURA_MAX_COPY_BYTES` is read as a positive integer or a refusal at startup (§17.209 (1)). `Serve.scripted` prints "`<Method> <path> -> <status> <body>`" for whatever `handle` returns. Decision: **(1) In the RFC, in 1.0, as phase 8s.** The non-goals bullet is rewritten: `Bun.serve`'s upgrade is delivered as `WebSocket.accept`; the other Bun-specific surfaces (`Bun.file`, `ArrayBufferSink`, TCP/UDP, FFI) stay out. RFC §1 gains the row "`WebSocket` (server, `Bun.serve` upgrade) | none | `std/websocket.accept` inside a `Serve` handler | `WebSocket` | `net` (the listener's) | ✓ | host | refuse until ported", and §2.10 is its shape. `std/websocket` enters the STABILITY inventory with `accept` and the topics in it, stable from 1.0.0 as RFC §Compatibility says of the additive modules. **(2) `accept` is an operation of `WebSocket`, not of `Serve`.** `fn accept<e>(req: Request, options: Upgrade, body: fn(Socket) -> Unit ! e) -> Response ! {Fail<SocketError> | e} requires options.max_message > 0`: when `req` is a served upgrade request that `handshake` admits, the host writes the 101, runs `body` with the socket under the performer's handlers (§5.5), closes the socket with 1001 on every exit of `body` as `connect` does (`file_closing`), and returns `Response { status: 101, headers: [], body: Empty }` so the handler's type is met; **the server discards what the handler returns for a connection it upgraded**, and a 101 returned for a connection that was not upgraded is the invalid response it is today (`D091`, answered 500). `Upgrade = { subprotocol: Option<String>, origins: List<String>, headers: List<(String, String)>, max_message: Int }`, `WebSocket.upgrade() -> Upgrade` = `{ None, [], [], 16_777_216 }`. The socket's operations are the client's: `send`, `receive`, `close`, `messages`, `protocol`, `closable`, `Message`, `Received`, `CloseInfo`, the same host functions over the same table entry. Why on `WebSocket`: one effect owns a socket's operations, so the handler that serves `send` on an accepted socket is the one that serves it on a connected one; `Socket` stays opaque in one module; `scripted` is one peer for both roles. `net` is unchanged: `Serve.host()` admitted the listener, `accept` opens nothing, and a `main` that accepts declares `{Serve, WebSocket}` and installs both hosts; the empty-`net` exit 75 of §17.286 (10) stands, since such a `main` could not listen either. **(3) The handshake is pure Sakura, shared.** `pub fn handshake(req: Request) -> Result<Handshake, String>`, `Handshake = { key: String, subprotocols: List<String>, origin: Option<String> }`, RFC 6455 §4.2.1 read strictly: method `Get`; a `host` header; `upgrade` a token list containing `websocket` (case-insensitive); `connection` containing the token `upgrade` (case-insensitive); `sec-websocket-key` 24 characters of Base64 decoding to 16 bytes (`Bytes.from_base64`, strict); `sec-websocket-version` exactly `13`; `req.body` is `Empty` (a `content-length` other than `0` or a `transfer-encoding` is refused, the host never reads an upgrade request's body); `sec-websocket-protocol` split on commas and trimmed, each a token, none repeated; `origin`, when present, ASCII-lowercased (RFC 6454 serializes it so). Each refusal is one string naming the header ("`sec-websocket-version` is not 13"). `accept` performs `handshake` first and fails `Accept(reason)` with its string; a handler that wants to answer 426 with `sec-websocket-version: 13`, or 404, or 403, calls `handshake` itself first and `accept` after. **(4) `SocketReason` gains `Accept(String)`**, the fifth variant: no upgrade happened, and why: a `handshake` refusal, "origin `o` is not accepted", "subprotocol `p` was not offered", "the socket limit of N is reached", "not a served upgrade request" (performed outside a served task, on a request whose connection is not an upgrade or is already answered, or a second `accept` on one request), or the host's failure string. The strings carry the peer's own header bytes (its origin, its subprotocol) and nothing else; a handler may send them back as a 4xx body. **(5) `origins` fails closed for browsers.** A request carrying `origin` whose value is not in `options.origins` (ASCII-lowercased on both sides, no wildcard, no pattern) is `Accept("origin … is not accepted")`; a request without `origin` is admitted, since only a browser sends one and a non-browser's `origin` is a string it chose. The empty default refuses every browser: cross-site WebSocket hijacking is the one attack the handshake itself invites (a browser sends the victim's cookies with the upgrade, RFC 6455 §10.2), and a list that starts empty is how `net` starts. Authentication stays the handler's (`authorization`, a cookie, a token in the path), as RFC §2.3 says of `Serve`. **(6) The subprotocol is the handler's choice.** `subprotocol: Some(p)` must be one of `Handshake.subprotocols` (else `Accept`) and is echoed in `sec-websocket-protocol`; `None` sends no header; `Socket.protocol` reads it on both ends. `Upgrade.headers` go on the 101 after the refusal of `WS_OWN` and any `sec-websocket-*` name (the client's rule, §17.286 (10d)), so a `set-cookie` may ride on the upgrade as in Bun. **(7) The wire in the server role.** No extension is negotiated: a `sec-websocket-extensions` offer is ignored and nothing is echoed, so the reserved bits stay 1002; no `permessage-deflate` (a compression oracle beside a credential on one connection, and a second bound to state; Bun's default is off too). Server frames are unmasked (RFC 6455 §5.1) and a client frame without a mask fails the connection with 1002; one parser, one framer, a role flag on the table entry (`wsFrame(op, payload, masked)`, `wsData` unmasking in place when `s.server`). Everything else is the client's rule verbatim, §17.286 (10) (e)–(g) read in the server role: 1009 before the payload is held, 1007, the fragment rules, the queue of 64 messages or `max_message` bytes then `pause`, the pong only while writable, the 5 s close timer, `file_closing` on every exit, 1001. The runtime sends no ping in either role (`sendPings` is not mirrored): liveness is the program's, as (8) says of idleness. **(8) Limits.** `max_message` per accepted socket (default 16 MiB, Bun's `maxPayloadLength`), the receive queue and `send`'s wait for drain as the client's. **One socket limit for both roles: `SAKURA_MAX_SOCKETS`**, default 1,024, read as `SAKURA_MAX_COPY_BYTES` is (a positive integer or a refusal at startup, §17.209 (1)), counting the open sockets in the instance's file table of both roles; at the limit `accept` is `Accept("the socket limit of 1024 is reached")` (the cookbook answers 503 with `retry-after`) and `connect` is `Connect(…)` with the same string, an additive bound on phase 8. **No idle timer in the runtime**: an idle policy is `Task.timeout(limit, fn() { WebSocket.receive(sock) })` around the wait, one visible line, the cancelled receive leaving the socket open (the host clears `waiter`); Bun's hidden 120 s close is not mirrored. TCP keepalive is enabled on every socket of both roles (`setKeepAlive(true)`, the OS interval), so a vanished peer surfaces as 1006 instead of a held slot. **(9) Topics: `subscribe`, `unsubscribe`, `publish`, in the host.** `fn subscribe(sock: Socket, topic: String) -> Unit ! {Fail<SocketError>} requires String.len(topic) <= 256`, `fn unsubscribe(sock, topic)` the same, `fn publish(topic: String, message: Message, except: Option<Socket>) -> Int ! {Fail<SocketError>} requires String.len(topic) <= 256`: the host keeps `topic → set of socket ids` per instance; `publish` writes `message`'s frame to every open subscribed socket but `except` (Bun's `ws.publish` excludes the sender, `server.publish` no one; one function with the choice as an argument), **never waits**, skips a subscriber whose write buffer already holds `max_message` bytes or more (Bun's `backpressureLimit` read as that socket's `max_message`, `closeOnBackpressureLimit` false: the message is missed, the socket kept) and skips one whose `max_message` the message exceeds, and returns the number of sockets written to; a socket's subscriptions end with its table entry (`file_close`'s step). On a socket that is closing or closed, `subscribe` is `NotOpen`. A topic is a `String` of at most 256 bytes by `requires` (`D020` at the perform site, §17.286 (8)); the number of topics is the program's, since only its code subscribes. Instance-local: a worker's instance (phase 11) has its own map, and cross-instance delivery is `Worker.topic`'s, experimental. Why the host: `V6003` is right (a socket must not outlive its body) and it makes a fan-out unwritable in Sakura, so the one place that can hold every open socket is the table that already does. **(10) Delivery of upgrade requests and the refusal path.** `serveHttp` adds an `upgrade` listener: the same `Request` is built (method, path, `rawHeaders`, body `Empty`, nothing read), `handle` runs as a task as for any request, and the raw socket plus `head` are held by the task (JS: a map by `ctx.t`; WASM: beside the reply in `served`, the guest naming its task as `serve_respond` does). `ws_accept` finds the connection by the performing task, computes `sec-websocket-accept`, writes the 101 (`upgrade`, `connection: Upgrade`, `sec-websocket-accept`, `sec-websocket-protocol` when chosen, the filtered `Upgrade.headers`, nothing from the request echoed), makes the table entry with `head` as the client's `wsOpen` does, and answers `Ok((id, protocol))`. A handler that returns without accepting is answered on the raw socket by the host: the status line, the response's headers, `content-length`, `connection: close`, the body, then `end`; whether through a `ServerResponse` assigned to the socket or a serialized head is the implementer's, with one runtime test per path. The stop (503) and the 405 of unknown methods apply as in `serveHttp`; a failure or defect in the handler before `accept` is a 500 by the same path; after the 101 a defect's record is written to stderr and the socket is closed by `file_closing` with 1001 (one close rule for both roles). The `Serve` effect, `serve.sak` and `serveHttp`'s outcomes are unchanged in shape; `serve.sak`'s header gains one sentence. **(11) ABI and the number.** New `hosted` imports `ws_accept(task, ptr, len)` (the tuple `(Handshake, Upgrade)`; `Result<(Int, String), String>`), `ws_subscribe(id, topic)`, `ws_unsubscribe(id, topic)` (`Result<Bool, String>`, `Ok(false)` once closing or closed) and `ws_publish(ptr, len)` (`(topic, Message, Option<Int>)`; `Result<Int, String>`), Node host only in `WASM_HOSTED` like `ws_close`; none of kind `secret`; nothing shipped changes. One MINOR, inside the phase's commit, with `test_bench.py`'s assertion and `sakura_abi_version` on both hosts (§17.270 (2)). The number is §17.266 (1)'s: 1.9.0 is 7b-W's; **the first of 8s and phase 10 to be ready takes 1.10.0 and the other 1.11.0 after it lands**, as §17.286 (12) ordered 7b-W and 10; §17.288 (10)'s "phase 10 takes 1.10.0" is read as that rule with 8s added to the pair. **(12) Order and lane.** 8s edits `websocket.sak`, `serve.sak` (comments), `sakura_core::builtins`, the WebSocket section and `serveHttp` of `sakura_runtime.js`, `served` in `sakura_wasm_host.js`, `WASM_HOSTED`, `validate.rs`, ABI.md, fixtures, `websocket.test.js`, `tests/wasm.rs`, `cli.rs` if a manifest fixture is added, `CHANGELOG.md`; phase 6 edits `compress.sak`, `rt` and the scheduler, phase 10 the scheduler and `rt`, 7c `crypto.sak` and the crypto sections. Disjoint but for `sakura_runtime.js` by section and the ABI number by (11), so **8s starts now in its own lane if an implementer is free, else after phase 6 in the web lane; before 10 in either case** (both are in the 1.0 contract; 8s is the smaller and completes a module whose other half is on `main`); 11 after 10; **7c runs in its own lane now** under its §17.288 (6) deadline, its lock hunk by §17.286 (12)'s rule. The web lane's order reads 7b-W, 6, 8s, 10, 11; §17.285's rule for a shared file stands. **(13) `scripted` plays the peer for `accept` as for `connect`.** Its `accept` clause runs `handshake`, the origin and subprotocol checks of (5) and (6), then `body` with a `Peer` from `script`; `subscribe`/`unsubscribe` keep a map; `publish` meets each subscribed scripted socket as a send does (the next `Reply`'s `expect`, else `Failed` naming the step) and returns the count. `pub fn upgrade_request(path: String, subprotocols: List<String>) -> Request`, pure, builds a request with the handshake headers (`host: example.test`, the RFC's sample key `dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==`, version 13, the protocol header when the list is not empty, no `origin`; a test adds one with `Request.with_header`), so `Serve.scripted([WebSocket.upgrade_request("/ws", [])])` with `WebSocket.scripted(script)` around `Serve.listen` is a three-backend fixture whose output is "`Get /ws -> 101 `" and the body's `Test.output`. **(14) Native.** Both effects are refused at startup today and stay so; the row that ports `WebSocket` natively (N1b's serve item, `m5-native.md` §2, with `rt`'s parser in both roles) ports both roles; no new row, no text change there now. **(15) Acceptance.** Fixtures: `websocket_accept_scripted_echo.sak`, `websocket_accept_rejects_handshake.sak` (method, `upgrade`, `connection`, key, version, body, each case one `Accept` string, under `Serve.scripted`), `websocket_accept_rejects_origin.sak`, `websocket_accept_rejects_subprotocol.sak`, `websocket_accept_rejects_max_message.sak` (`expect-defect: D020`, the perform span), `websocket_publish_scripted_fanout.sak` (two accepted sockets, one `except`, the `Int`), `websocket_publish_rejects_topic_length.sak` (`D020`), a UI fixture `V6003` for a socket escaping `accept`'s body; each with `// Spec: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#section-…`. `websocket.test.js`, a Sakura-served server against Node's global `WebSocket` and the raw client of `ws_peer.mjs`'s kind: text, binary, fragmented, ping/pong, an unmasked client frame 1002, 1009, 1007, close 1000 in both directions, 1001 on `body`'s return, the refusal path (a `GET` with `Upgrade: h2c` gets the handler's response with `connection: close`; a plain `GET` on the route gets its response), the 426 cookbook refusal carrying `sec-websocket-version: 13`, an origin refused as 403 and one admitted, the subprotocol echoed, an extension offer not echoed, `SAKURA_MAX_SOCKETS=1` making the second accept `Accept(…)` → 503, two clients subscribed and `except`, the backpressure skip (a subscriber that does not read, the predicate on `writableLength` unit-tested if the TCP buffer cannot be filled deterministically). `tests/wasm.rs::websocket_accept_on_wasm_as_on_js`: one served program, same output and trace on JS and WASM. `cli.rs`: `net = []` exit 75 unchanged. ABI.md §0 and §8.2's WebSocket paragraph at the new MINOR; `std/INDEX.md` regenerated. Docs (phase 12): the stdlib page, `cookbook/websocket_server.mdx` (Opus, a code fence: the route, `handshake` then `accept`, `origins`, the 426/403/503 answers, a `Task.timeout` idle), the RFC's server example, `manifest.mdx` one sentence (`net` covers the listener; `accept` adds no entry). Why: the shape is phase 8's with the roles swapped, so every rule the client already has is reused and the two new facts (the handshake and who holds every socket) are the only new code; a pure handshake is testable on three backends without a connection; `origins` and the socket limit are the fail-closed bounds AGENTS.md asks for, in the attacker's units; topics live in the host because the language's own resource rule forbids the alternative; the handler returning a `Response` it never sends is one odd line, and the alternatives each cost a type or a closure in a value. Rejected: `accept` on `Serve` (the effect that opened the listener, not the socket's operations; a cross-module `Socket` constructor; a 0.2.0 change to every user `handler Serve` for nothing); a third effect (`Upgrade`) for one operation; `open`/`message`/`close` callbacks (RFC 0002: no event listeners; a message is a value `receive` returns); a `Response` variant carrying the body closure (a value with a closure, and `Serve.scripted` could not print it); routing by a second listener instead of the handler (the handler decides per request, as Bun's `fetch` does); the `ws` package; `permessage-deflate`; a wildcard or pattern origin; admitting a browser by default (Bun's behaviour, and the attack of (5)); a runtime idle timer (a close the program did not write); runtime pings (`sendPings`); 1011 on a defect exit (one close rule, the record is on stderr); a `publish` that waits for every subscriber (one slow peer stalls every publisher) or closes one (Bun keeps it, and a close the program did not ask for); holding sockets in handler state (`V6003` stands); cross-instance publish (phase 11's `Worker.topic`); a per-socket topic cap (only the program subscribes); landing 8s in two commits with two MINORs (one phase, one number); holding 8s behind 10 (both are 1.0's and their files are disjoint); holding 7c for the web lane (its deadline is the window, its files are its own). Performance: one unmask loop per client frame, already paid by the client role for its own frames; `publish` is one `write` per subscriber and a `Set` lookup; the socket counter is one integer; nothing on a counted program's path. Changed: RFC 0002 §Non-goals (the bullets), the guide-level section (a server example after the client's), §1 (the row), §2.10 (new), §4 (`Accept`), §5 (`scripted` covers `accept` and `publish`), §6 (the row), §Security (the handshake bullet), §Tests, §Implementation and rollout, §Metadata; `web-apis.md` §2 (the row, the order paragraph), phase 8s (new), §4 (one line), §5; the §17 heading. Impact: Opus, one commit in its own lane or after phase 6: the std module, the runtime, the WASM host and ABI at the number (11) gives, the fixtures and runtime tests of (15), the changelog, the cookbook page; 7c's implementer starts in a second lane. The owner: one review of the served-upgrade path as §17.286 (10) was, a dated line under the REQUESTS entry: (a) `handshake` pure and shared, each refusal one string; (b) `origins` empty refuses every browser, no wildcard; (c) the refusal response is written by the host with `connection: close` and echoes no request header; (d) the 101 carries only the four handshake headers and the filtered `Upgrade.headers`; (e) the parser's role flag, an unmasked client frame 1002, no extension echoed; (f) `SAKURA_MAX_SOCKETS` counts both roles and refuses an invalid value at startup; (g) topics instance-local, subscriptions end with the socket, `publish` never waits; (h) the `Accept` strings carry the peer's own bytes and no other header; (i) `ws_accept` answers only for the performing task's own upgrade request, once; (j) no dependency added. Sol: phase 12 for `accept` (the stdlib page, the inventory row's text, `llms.txt`, the gap row of `Bun.serve` rewritten as delivered). Nothing for Astra.

290. **WS-P21's soundness review: the owned-elements fact and the `set(bs, j, {..bj})` site (`1b7636e0`) are ratified with one hole closed now — a `bs[i]` read (`list_get`) retains an element in an `Option` the liveness never sees, so it is a retaining use, allowed only where nothing of the chain is live after; the second shape (`f39be4ac`, `b = {..b, …}` once `b` is no longer the element) is unsound as landed, on two counterexamples, and is reverted today, re-landed only with every holder on its origin path linear and every read it tests against bound outside every join that carries `b`; the five implementer readings are ratified; the differential generator gains the three shapes it was blind to; WS-P21 is accepted below its exit as the bucket reachable without `j > i`; WS-P16 starts when `main` is sound (CODEOWNERS; §17.149, §17.201 (3), §17.273, §17.276, §17.278; plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1; `bench/deltas.md` row WS-P21; round 43, 2026-10-21).** Facts: the landed analysis (`opt/owned/elems.rs`) computes the fact per *chain* (the versions of one list in a def: an owned update's result and its consumed argument, a join parameter and its arguments, one object on JS); a chain owns its elements when every version came from a fresh-element origin, every update is owned and stores a moved fresh record or puts the element read at an index back at that same index, every other use of a version or of an element local retains nothing or happens when nothing of the chain is live after it, and an element local flows only into join parameters that are element locals of the chain; an element local is one bound by `list_at`, `list_get_expect` or an `elem_read` def on a version, or an alias or join parameter of one; liveness is Core liveness over *record and list locals only* (`univ`). The site reuses `bj`'s object and guards against every live element local of the chain (at most two). The counts: `nbody` n = 100,000 on Node 687.4 M → 623.6 M (the site, −9.3%) → 581.6 M (with the second shape, −15.4%), exit 25%; the −32% §17.273 cited was the unguarded reuse of both records, sound only under `j > i`, which §17.273 rejected proving. The review built and ran three programs through `sakura run` (direct) and `sakura run --no-direct` (CPS, the persistent reading, since the emitter reuses in direct code only); the two disagree on all three. **CE1, the ruled site**: `fn kick(start, j) { var bs = start; let o = bs[j]; let c = at(bs, j); bs = List.set(bs, j, Body { ..c, v: c.v + 10 }); let old = match o { Some(b) => b.v, None => -1 }; List.push(bs, Body { x: old, v: 0 }) }` on `[{3,0}, {4,0}]`, `j = 1`: `--dump owned` prints `kick consumes start with elements`, `rec = Body {..r} allocates, owned entry in place`; direct prints `ys 3:0 4:10 10:0`, `--no-direct` `ys 3:0 4:10 0:0`. `bs[j]` lowers to `list_get`, which is in `BORROWS` (it retains no node of the *list*, the §17.149 fact), so `list_use_ok` counts it a read; its `Option<Body>` is neither a record nor a list local, so it is not in `after`, not an element local, not guarded; the fused `list_get_expect` is the only form the analysis sees as an element read. **CE2, the second shape, a holder that is not linear**: `var b = at(start, 0); while k < steps { let box = Box { body: b }; b = Body { ..b, v: b.v + 1 }; boxes = List.push(boxes, box); k = k + 1 }` on `[{1,0}]`, three steps: dump `rec = Body {..b} in place unless b is r`; direct `boxes 0 3 3`, `--no-direct` `boxes 0 1 2`. The join parameter `b` has class `Elem` by the meet of the read and the fresh rebuild, and an `Elem` class is never required to be linear; `moved_site` reads only the *origins* of `b` (`origins`), never its uses, and checks no chain fact, so the box's reference to the moved record is invisible and the rebuild writes into it. **CE4, the second shape, every holder linear**: `var bs = start; var b = at(bs, 1); while i < 3 { let r = at(bs, 1); boxes = List.push(boxes, Box { body: r }); if i == 1 { b = r }; while k < m_i { b = Body { ..b, v: b.v + 1 } }; bs = List.set(bs, 1, Body { x: i, v: 0 }) }` with `m = [2, 0, 3]`, then `boxes[1].body.v`: dump `rec = Body {..b} in place unless b is r%2 or r%18`; direct `box1 3`, `--no-direct` `box1 0`. At the third iteration `b` still holds the second iteration's `r` (the inner loop ran zero times, `b` was carried round the outer join), while the guard compares against this iteration's `r`, a different object: the doc comment's premise, "each such read is bound before `bj`, so the value it holds at `x` is the one that may have reached `bj`", is false for a read bound inside a loop whose parameter carries `bj` across iterations; the index-renaming in `incoming` does not catch it because both reads are at the literal `1`. The ruled site is not open to CE4's shape: its guards are *every* live element local of the chain whatever value each holds, and its `bj` names the slot's object by the index it was read at. The differential run (2,000 programs with the reuse on, 2,000 with `SAKURA_DIFF_ELEMENTS=0`) passed because its generator writes `spread_p` and `drift_p` only, the two fixtures' shapes; `audit_owned` would have stopped on CE1, CE2 and CE4 (each reads a reused record later), so the oracle is sound and was blind. The generic std defs (`List.set`, `List.map`) are analysed with a type variable as a possible record and cannot hold a site (no concrete record type to allocate); their `keeps_elems`/`stores` and `fresh_elems_cb` are consumed only at a caller whose instantiation is a `List` of records. Closure lambdas are callees in the summary order, so a callback's `fresh_value` exists before `List.map`'s caller is summarised; a recursive component starts from no claim and iterates up, a least fixpoint. Decision: **(1) An element put back at the index it was read from keeps the fact, ratified.** The index is the same Core local or literal, followed through join parameters by `incoming`, so the object goes back into the one slot it may still occupy; whatever that slot holds then is dropped from the list (an element local may still name it, and a later site on that local writes an object no slot holds). No object ever sits in two slots. **(2) A retaining use is allowed when nothing of the chain is live after it, ratified, with "live" named and one hole closed.** "Live" is Core liveness over the def's record and list locals; the rule is sound because a site needs a live version to store into, and every tracked way back into the chain (an alias, a projection of a carrier) is a poisoned origin. The hole is a use that retains an element in a value that is not a tracked local: `list_get`, the one `BORROWS` builtin whose result holds an element. **The fix, Opus, `fix(core)`, now, one commit:** in `elems.rs` `list_use_ok`, a read counts as retaining nothing only when its result holds no element or is itself an element local of the chain — `list_len`, `list_contains`, `list_at`, `list_get_expect` and an `elem_read` def, not `list_get`, which falls to `last` (allowed at a last position, else the chain is disowned); `BORROWS` itself is unchanged (list ownership is unaffected, the `Option` shares no node). The ruled site's argument then holds as the module doc states it: the object in `bj` is referenced by its slot, by `bj` and by element locals of the chain, and by nothing else. Fixture `owned_elements_option.sak` (CE1 verbatim, expected `ys 3:0 4:10 0:0`), both ABIs, WASM, the LIR corpus, `--dump owned` pinned (the element arm allocates; `kick` loses `with elements`). **(3) A type variable as a possible record, ratified** (the facts above: the generic def can prove only what a concrete caller discharges, and cannot host a site). **(4) Lambdas as callees in summary order, ratified**; the least-fixpoint start for a recursive component is the sound direction for a freshness claim. **(5) In place in direct mode only, ratified**: a CPS continuation carries live locals only, the plain allocation is always right, and `--no-direct` is the persistent reading every element fixture's expected output is taken from. **(6) The second shape is reverted today and re-landed under two added conditions.** Opus: `git revert f39be4ac` as the first commit of the lane (it is separately revertible by design; `owned_elements_moved.sak` goes with it and comes back with the re-land); the fix of (2) second. The re-land (`perf(core)`, citing this entry) keeps `moved_site` and `origins` with: **(i)** every node `origins` visits that is not a read — each join parameter and each alias on the path to `bj` — is `linear` (every use a read, or a store, jump or return after which it is dead), so a fresh record reaching `bj` was only ever moved and `bj` is its one reference; **(ii)** every read in the guard set is bound before (lexically outside) every `LetJoin` whose parameter is on the path, so a read's current value is the value that reached `bj` — a value carried across a loop's back edge can only ride a parameter of that loop or of an enclosing one, which (ii) then forces the read outside; otherwise no site. The argument, written into the `moved_site` doc: at `x`, `bj` holds a read's current object (excluded by its guard) or a fresh object with one reference. `nbody`'s pin keeps `rec%64 = Body {..b%19} in place unless b%19 is r%11` (its `b` is linear, its `r` is bound outside the inner loop). Fixtures `owned_elements_boxed.sak` (CE2, expected `boxes 0 1 2`) and `owned_elements_carried.sak` (CE4, expected `box1 0`), both ABIs, WASM, the LIR corpus, `--dump owned` pinned (`allocates` for both). The re-land goes before WS-P16 if it is green in the same session, else right after; it needs no further review beyond its pins reading as written here. **(7) The differential generator gains the three shapes**: a `bs[i]` `Option` held across the update and matched after it, a moved record stored (a `Box` or a `push`) before its rebuild, and a rebuild carried across an outer loop with the read inside it; each with the reuse on and off. An oracle sees only what its generator writes; a soundness change's packet names the shapes its argument excludes and the generator writes them. **(8) WS-P21's exit, re-read as §17.287 read WS-W5's: the bucket.** The row's bucket is `advance`'s twenty rebuilds a step; the ruled site reuses ten, the second shape six more, and the four that remain (the first rebuild of `b` after each read) are reachable only with `j > i`, which §17.273 rejected; the 25% was sized on the unguarded hand edit and was this entry's error to correct, not the implementer's to meet. **Accepted as landed below its exit, counted at −9.3% on `main` after the revert and at the re-land's number after it** (the row's "after" cell is re-counted then, one worktree, one session). The remaining arm on `nbody`, the five bodies `List.map`'s callback rebuilds a step (an owned entry of `List.map` whose callback parameter is an owned element), is named here and not opened: it is a third mechanism for about a fifth of the bucket, and the JS lane's next rows are the ones §17.276 ordered. **(9) WS-P16 starts when `main` is sound**: after the revert and the (2) fix are on `main` (the same files, the same agent, as planned). Why: a soundness review's product is the counterexample, and three ran; (2)'s hole is one `BORROWS` member read for a fact it was never a fact about, closed in one line; the second shape's guard argument is the ruled site's borrowed without the chain fact that made it work, and (i) and (ii) are the two things the chain fact was providing (no other holder, no stale read); reverting first keeps every commit on `main` sound while the re-land is written, and the pins carry the re-land's review. Rejected: keeping `f39be4ac` on `main` while it is fixed (a known unsound reuse on `main`, however briefly, when the revert is one command); fixing CE1 by tracking `Option<Body>` locals in the liveness (a container analysis for one builtin's result, when the use can simply retain); proving `j > i` for the four remaining rebuilds (§17.273's rejection stands); dropping the second shape for good (−6% on `nbody` from six reuses a step, and the general shape of a record rebuilt in a loop, with a fifteen-line condition); raising the row's exit to carry it (the mechanism's bucket is counted and the gap is named). Performance: none until the re-land; (2)'s fix disowns only chains with a `bs[i]` `Option` live across an update (no benchmark has one). Changed: this entry; plan `performance-r1.md` §4.1 (the WS-P21 paragraph: ruled; WS-P16's trigger). Impact: Opus, in order: the revert; `fix(core)` with `owned_elements_option.sak`; the re-land with (i), (ii), `owned_elements_boxed.sak` and `owned_elements_carried.sak`; the generator's three shapes (inside the fix or the re-land); the `bench/deltas.md` row re-counted; then WS-P16. Nothing for Sol or Astra.

292. **Dogfood 1 (`dispatch-packlist`, `10140219`) triaged against `main`: five of its fourteen items block `v1.0.0-beta.1`, each a wrong promise or a shape the breaking window would otherwise close over — `Cli.exit` on WASM is wired to the guest's existing exit outcome (no new host import), `Json.parse`/`Json.decode` syntax errors become one content-free message on every backend, `Violation.clause` becomes the failing top-level conjunct's text as `std/core` has promised since §4.3, `Path`'s refinement refuses `\` and `:`, and `Console` gains `eprint` (an ABI MINOR under §17.289 (11)'s rule); `Violation` enters the prelude with the clause fix; duplicate JSON keys stay last-value-at-first-position and are documented; a failure escaping `main` keeps exit 1 as STABILITY.md already says; the rest is beta.N, `sakura doc`'s name forms first; RFC 0002 §2.7 is corrected: since 7a-W/7b-W the WASM-on-Node host signs ECDSA through `node:crypto`, so only native is RFC 6979 (owner's delegation while asleep; §17.17, §17.254, §17.255, §17.262 (3), §17.288 (2), §17.289 (11), §17.291 (1b)–(1c), (3f); `dogfood/dispatch-packlist/FRICTION.md`, `src/main.sak`; plan `road-to-1.0.md` stage 5; RFC 0002 §2.7; round 44, 2026-10-21).** Facts: the program was written by Claude Opus 5.5 in a fresh session against the installed `sakura 0.1.0` (`2014e821`) with no checkout, as §17.255 (1) requires; it checked clean on the first try and 23 of 24 tests passed on the first run. Each friction item re-read on `main` today: (1) `Cli.exit` under `sakura run --target wasm` is still `D090` "builtin cli_exit is not supported by the WASM backend yet" (`sakura_codegen_wasm/src/func.rs` line 1723's fallback), while the guest runtime already has everything but the builtin: `Exec::exit` (`rt/src/exec.rs` line 1171: unwinds every finalizer, ends the task `EXIT`), the `EXIT` outcome with its `u32` code (`exports.rs` lines 159, 198), the Node host's `OUTCOME.exit` case (`sakura_wasm_host.js` line 1449, `{ kind: "exit", code }`), the WASI `_start`'s kind-5 branch (`wasi.rs` line 189) and the signature `cli_exit: (i64) -> unit` in `sakura_lir/src/builtins.sigs` line 12; what is missing is one `rt_b_cli_exit` row in `exports.rs`'s builtin table (line 1601 onward), so no host import and no ABI MINOR is involved; `std/INDEX.md` line 10 says every module runs on both backends and names only `std/crypto`'s primitives. (2) `json_parse` in `sakura_runtime.js` line 3129 returns `Err(DecodeError("", String(e.message)))`, V8's text, which quotes a prefix of the body (`Unexpected token 'o', "not json at"... is not valid JSON`) and changes with Node's version; `rt/src/json.rs` `syntax()` (line 446) writes `Unexpected token 'X' in JSON at position N`, `Unexpected end of JSON input` or `JSON nested too deeply`, and its own comment says parity does not compare a host's syntax message: the two backends already disagree on a `Result` a program can print, and `Json.decode` shares the parse. (3) `Cli.parse` of a variant-typed flag accepts the constructor's exact spelling only and the usage shows `<value>` (`sakura_runtime.js` lines 3325, 3859; `json.rs` lines 1117, 2357). (4) `sakura_core/src/lower/expr.rs` line 667 builds every `Violation` with `clause: "where"`; `std/core.sak` lines 8–9 promise "the source text of the failing conjunct" with the example `it <= 100`; `sakura_analysis/src/specs.rs` already renders a refinement as `("where", "it >= 0 && it <= 100")` (line 383) for `--frozen-specs`, and `sakura_hir/src/lower.rs` line 1482 holds the `WHERE_CLAUSE` node when it lowers the predicate. (5) `std/path.sak` `is_relative` refuses `""`, a leading `/` and a `..` segment only; `a\..\b`, `C:\x` and `\\server\share` pass, and the comment above says "a handler rooted at a directory cannot be escaped through one"; the JS host's `fs_subdir` resolves and checks containment (`within`, line 3563, by `path.sep`), so the escape is stopped one layer down on every OS, but Windows is a supported platform (P5, P8) where `\` is the separator and `C:` a drive, so the refinement's sentence is false there; `a/./b`, `a//b` and `a/` are accepted and harmless (`of` and `join` normalise them; `validate` returns the string as given). (6) `Dir.subdir`'s doc comment (`fs.sak` line 79) does not say `name` may hold several segments; the grant check is on the directory opened, so `subdir(root, "data")` under `fs.read = ["./data/clean"]` fails by design. (7) `Fs.memory` takes `(Path, Bytes)` only; a directory exists while a file is inside it, as its doc says. (8) `Fs.list` is "Entries sorted by name" on every handler, the determinism contract. Decision, one per item (repeated in each `FRICTION.md` as a dated `Triage:` line): **MT-1: bug, security-relevant (a capability read outside `Env`, the manifest grant and the test's empty environment; a machine-dependent cassette key), beta-blocking, Breaking since 0.1.0.** The process-environment read is deleted. `Llm.anthropic(key, model)` always sends to `https://api.anthropic.com`; a new `Llm.anthropic_at(base: Url, key: Secret<String>, model: Model) -> Handler<Llm, {Budget, Http}>` sends to `<base>/v1/messages` (the host's `net` check applies to `base` as to any request), and `anthropic` is `anthropic_at(Url.parse("https://api.anthropic.com"), …)`. A program that wants the endpoint from its environment reads it under its own `Env` handler and manifest grant and passes it: `Llm.anthropic_at(Url.parse(Option.unwrap_or(Env.get("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL"), "https://api.anthropic.com")), key, model)`. `replay` and `recording` are unchanged (a recording under `anthropic` now keys on the canonical URL on every machine). `m3.rs` line 971 passes its port through `anthropic_at` in the program source; `ABI.md`'s sentence names the function instead of the variable; review A3's row gains "closed by §17.293". Migration line: "`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` is no longer read; pass the endpoint with `Llm.anthropic_at`". The shapes stay as they are: the API needs the wrapper, `scripted` is the Sakura-side value, and changing either breaks every test in the corpus for no gain. **MT-3: API gap, beta.N (additive).** The compiler lowers the recognisable top-level conjuncts of a `where` clause to schema keywords (`String.len(it) <= n`/`>= n` to `maxLength`/`minLength`, `List.len(it)` likewise to `maxItems`/`minItems`, `it <= n`/`>= n` on `Int` and `Float` to `maximum`/`minimum`, `String.matches(it, "re")` to `pattern`; anything else omitted) and `jsonSchemaJs` emits them beside the base; decoding keeps checking the predicate; `apiSchema` keeps the keywords the API accepts. Decision, one per item (repeated in each `FRICTION.md` as a dated `Triage:` line): **RQ-1: duplicate of §17.292 (14) and §17.293 PQ-4.** The recipe is right for `main` and the beta; the beta's `sakura prompt` opens with its version and the site keeps "tracks `main`" with the changes page beside it; nothing else. **RQ-2: duplicate of §17.292 (11)**, with one doc word in lane B's running round: `transaction`'s comment reads "rolled back when it fails with any error, `SqlError` or the body's own". **RQ-3 (SS-5, WP-4): language gap, beta.N (additive), first in lane B's queue after §17.292 (11) and PQ-6.** `error` is accepted wherever a field name stands: a `FIELD_DECL`, a record literal's `name: expr` and `..` update, a record pattern's field, and the name after `.`; the token stays `ERROR_KW` and item position keeps dispatching it to `error_decl`, so no program changes meaning; `fmt` prints the name as written; `Json.encode`/`decode` and `Schema` see an ordinary field, so `type ErrorView = { error: String, message: String }` encodes as `{"error":…,"message":…}`. No raw-identifier syntax (`r#error`, backticks) is added: the one keyword three programs hit is `error`, and a general escape is a grammar feature for a problem one word has. Fixture `compiler/tests/semantics/error_field_name.sak` (declare, construct, update, match, access, encode; one `.stdout` on both backends) and a `fmt` case; the spec's grammar chapter gains the sentence "the keyword `error` is a valid field name" when it lands. **RQ-4: duplicate of §17.293 PQ-6 and MT-11b.** **RQ-5: tooling gap, beta.N (additive), second in the agent-DX queue after `sakura doc`.** `W1003 unused_import` (RESOLVE family, next free), one per unused imported name, with a `MachineApplicable` fix that removes the name (or the whole `import` line when nothing of it is used), so `sakura fix` applies it; a name used only in a type, a pattern or a `@contract_test` attribute is used; the skill's repair table gains the row. **RQ-6: API gap, beta.N (additive).** `Response.status_json<T: Schema>(code: Int, value: T) -> Response requires code >= 100 && code <= 599`: `ok_json`'s body and content type at `code`; `ok_json(value)` stays `status_json(200, value)`'s short form; the author's record-update spelling stays valid. **RQ-7: bug (an over-strict guard), beta.N.** `sakura test --record` with an empty `net` list runs with the grants it has: every host `Http.send` fails closed as under `run`, `Http.recording` appends what in-process handlers answer, and the refusal line becomes one note on stderr ("note: `[permissions] net` lists no host; recording captures in-process handlers only"); exit 75 stays for an invalid manifest's `V8006` path as today. The cassettes page gets the author's synthetic-cassette recipe now (lane D, beside MT-4's in-order handler): a throwaway test whose outer `Http` handler routes to the app over `Sql.memory()`, run once under `--record --filter`, then deleted; a cassette is regenerated by deleting it first. The Node warning is MT-11f (lane C). **RQ-8: by design, one doc sentence (lane D, capabilities page).** 75 is the manifest's shape check, by effect: `main` declares an effect and `[permissions]` grants it no list. A value outside a list, a host spelling the list does not carry (`localhost` is not `127.0.0.1`; the check resolves no name) or a path outside `fs.write`, fails at the operation with the effect's own error after whatever ran before it, so a program that must refuse early checks its configuration at the top of `main`. The brief's "same host spelling" rule is enforced at `Serve.listen`, and the author's `integration.sh` asserting 75, 75, 1 and 1 is the correct record. **RQ-9: by design (§17.102), one paragraph (lane D, testing page).** `sakura test` has no host grants and no mode with them; a program is tested against the host by running it (`sakura run`) and driving it from a script, as `repair-queue/integration.sh` does: start, request, stop by the listener's PID, restart, read back. The paragraph links the file. No `sakura test --host` mode: a test with grants is an integration run with a different name, and the grant model is the one thing §17.102 keeps simple. **RQ-10 (SS-S1–S3, WP-15): process, no toolchain item.** The briefs' version and migration steps are §17.291 (3c) and (1b): the programs ran on `v0.1.0`, Astra's `MIGRATION.md` is written against beta.1's notes when they exist, and the dated "skipped" sections are the correct record; cvc5 is optional (`cross_check: null` is a value, not a defect). **SS-S4 (WP-3): bug (help text), rider in lane B's running round.** `Setup`'s doc line becomes "List this project's agent files and, with `--apply`, write them: …" and `sakura setup --apply`'s behaviour is unchanged; `cli.txt` does not change (it pins arguments). An agent that may not write reads the skill at the site's `/skills` mirror and the guide at `sakura prompt`; no `--print` flag, since the skill is 7,000 words and the paths are what a dry run is for. **SS-1 (WP-1, WP-2): duplicate of §17.292 (11)**, with WP-2's facet folded into it: `sakura doc` of a std symbol loads std alone and never the current directory's tree; a project symbol needs the project. **SS-2 (WP-10): duplicate of §17.292 (14)**; `verify_summary` is on `main`. **SS-3: by design, one doc line (lane B's running round).** `Url`'s comment gains "A `Url` is a `String`: interpolate it or pass it where a `String` goes; `to_string` renders `UrlParts`". **SS-4: bug (a grammar inconsistency), beta.N (additive), lane B's queue.** A `type` item continues past newlines to a `where`, as a signature does to `requires`/`ensures` (`past_newlines`); `fmt` keeps writing `where` on the `type` line and breaking after it; the `V5003` cascade goes with the `V0001`. Instead the three texts are promised where `DecodeError`'s are (§17.292 (2)): `Http.host`'s comment says a host outside the manifest fails `HttpError { status: None, reason: "<host:port> is not in the manifest's net list" }`, `scoped`'s says `"<url> is outside Http.scoped"`, `Fs`'s comment says `"not in the manifest's fs.<read|write> list"` (the `Sql` error wraps it behind the file's name), and the capabilities page lists them; a test matches the text, as the author's does. `Http.is_refused(e: HttpError) -> Bool` is beta.N (additive) if a second program asks; a typed kind is a 2.0 shape or never. **SS-16: by design (§8.6, §16.13).** The timer gate is the pattern and the testing page's concurrency example shows it (lane D, one paragraph); §16.13's trigger is streaming between fibers, which a gate is not; a latch is after 1.0 if a program needs one, never a beta change. **SS-17: duplicate of §17.293 MT-8. One `ui` case with the author's `"{\"available\": 10,"` and exactly one diagnostic, on `--json` too (the agent-DX reading: 83 records for one byte is a context-window bug). **WP-6: duplicate of §17.293 PQ-6, a second shape folded into lane B's running fix.** When the unresolved name heads a `name: expr` statement of a brace expression, the diagnostic reads "a record literal names its type: `Circuit { request: 0, … }`" and offers no import. **WP-7: bug (verifier incompleteness: a true obligation `disproved`), beta.N, first in lane E.** A projection of a field whose declared type is refined assumes `T$check` on the projected value as `refined_params` does for a parameter (once per projection site, memoised on the path), and an input or parameter of record type assumes the checks of its refined fields; the author's probe is the fixture (`direct` and `field` both `proved`; a third function reading a refined field through a nested record). `verify` is a preview (STABILITY.md, "restricted fragment"), so this is not a gate; lane E starts now on its own files and lands in beta.1 if it is ready before the preparation commit, else beta.N. **WP-8: by design (modular summaries) with one lane E item, beta.N.** The `ensures` rule stands and the message names it; the `unsupported` on `match T.validate(v)` is lane E's second item: the encoder builds the join of `Ok(v)` with the predicate assumed and `Err(Violation)` with the payload opaque, so `watts ensures unchanged` is decided. **WP-9: bug, beta.N, lane E's third item.** `sakura verify` skips `test` bodies: a test is executed, never proved; its captured values are unconstrained inputs and an `expect_defect` call violates on purpose, so every obligation it yields is noise and `test$N` is a name nobody can map; the counts in `verify_summary` drop them; no flag (`sakura test --contracts` is the path a test takes). One fixture: a file with a function and a test that calls it with a violating literal, `verify` exits 0 with the function's obligations only. **WP-10: fixed on `main`** (§17.257), the docs half §17.292 (14). **WP-11, WP-12: duplicates of §17.292 (1) and (2).** **WP-13: doc gap, settled: WASM builds drop proved checks.** `tour/verification.mdx` line 48 reads "`run`, `test` and LIR output retain these checks; a WASM build drops the checks `sakura verify --target wasm` proved, as the JS build does for the `js` profile"; the 0.1.0 CHANGELOG line 578 gains the parenthetical "(superseded within this release by §17.163 (4) below: WASM builds drop proved checks)", history corrected in place and dated; the verify reference is already right. Why: none of the forty-three items is a wrong promise the beta would ship or a shape the window closes over, which is the test §17.291 and §17.292 set; the four riders cost nothing beyond the commits they join and each fixes a sentence or a message an agent reads; `error` as a field name is the one language change three independent sessions asked for, and it is additive, so it lands when lane B reaches it and the beta does not wait; WP-5 is the one agent-DX bug (83 `--json` records for one byte) and is ranked with it; the verifier's three items are real and belong in one lane that touches `sakura_verify` alone, so lane E runs beside the others from today and the tag does not wait for a preview feature; the refusal texts are promised rather than typed because the typed shape costs 52 sites and every user handler inside a window that is closing, for a distinction a documented string gives. 295. **Security review for `v1.0.0-beta.1`, delegated by the owner: the WebSocket client's `net` path (§17.286 (10) (a)–(k)) and the served-upgrade path (§17.289 (a)–(j)) are approved with one runtime fix that lands before the beta's preparation commit (after a close is known, a peer's further bytes are held without bound and the TCP socket is never destroyed outside the `ws_close` path) and one nit (the raw refusal path writes any status); the 7b crate set is approved and the dalek crates and `aes-gcm` gain their `zeroize` feature now (no new crate); phase 7c is approved: `oaepSeal` is RFC 8017 §7.1.1 step for step, its seed rule gains the word "unpredictable", the RSA import's CRT members are checked in a beta.N fix (OpenSSL's fault fallback hides a wrong `qi`, BoringSSL refuses it), the tier-2 readings are ratified, the `import_key` reachability cost is accepted without a split and becomes a perf-lane row's evidence; the `V9001` "unbound row variable r0" is reproduced, does not gate the beta, and is first in the beta.N queue (§17.286 (10), §17.288 (7), (8), (9), §17.289, §17.291, §17.292; `compiler/REQUESTS.md` the four entries; round 47, 2026-10-21).** Facts, from reading the code at `832509be`, not the lists. *Client* (`sakura_runtime.js` 5283–5758): (a) `ws_connect` runs `netRefusal(new URL(url))` (4192) before anything opens, after `checked_url` admitted `ws`/`wss` without a fragment; `u.hostname` keeps IPv6 brackets and is punycode for an IDN, the port defaults 443/80 by scheme; an empty `net` is exit 75 at startup, unchanged. (b) `req.on("response")` drains, destroys and answers `Err("the handshake answered N, not 101")`; Node emits `upgrade` for a response only at 101, so no second host is reachable. (c) `node:https.request` with `host`, `port`, `path`, `headers` only: `rejectUnauthorized` and the agent untouched, no proxy variable read; Node's own TLS honours `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` for every TLS socket of the process, `fetch` included, which the runtime neither reads nor can refuse (a fact, recorded). (d) `WS_OWN` and `sec-websocket-*` refused before the request, the rest passed to Node's `request`, whose validation throws inside the `try`; Node's `ERR_INVALID_CHAR` names the header, never its value, so a CR in an `authorization` value is `Err` with no credential in it. (e) 16 random bytes as the key, `sec-websocket-accept` compared, a chosen subprotocol only when offered, any `sec-websocket-extensions` refused, `wsFrame` draws a fresh 4-byte mask per client frame. (f) `wsData`: reserved bits, a masked frame in the client role or an unmasked one in the server role, an unknown opcode, a fragmented or long control frame and a misplaced continuation are 1002; `s.size + len > s.max` is 1009 before the payload is held, the 64-bit length past `max_message` read as `Infinity`; text and a close reason are checked by `TextDecoder` fatal (1007); a one-byte close payload 1002; fragment state resets per message. (g) `wsFull` is 64 messages or more than `max_message` waiting bytes, `pause`/`resume` around it; a pong only while `!writableNeedDrain`; `ws_close` arms `WS_CLOSE_MS` then `destroy`; `unref` after `end`; `suspend`'s cancel destroys the handshake request and closes an opened socket. (h) `failureOf` is the message only; the strings carry the status, the subprotocol the server chose, nothing else. (i) `std/websocket.sak` declares nine externals, all `ws_*` and `file_closing`; `scripted` and `checked_url` call none. (j) `ws_peer.mjs` listens on `127.0.0.1`, port 0. (k) builtin modules only. **The finding:** `wsEnd` (5606) sets `closed`, calls `socket.end()` and `unref()`, and nothing more; `wsData` (5510) appends every chunk to `s.buf` before testing `s.closed`, and its loop runs only while `closed === null`. So once a close is known by any path but `ws_close`'s (the peer's close frame, or our own 1002/1007/1009 fail), a peer that keeps sending grows `s.buf` by every byte it sends, nothing consumes it, and the socket is never destroyed (`end` is a FIN; `http.Server` sockets are `allowHalfOpen`, and a client socket reads on until the peer's FIN). `wsFree` (5690) ends, never destroys, so the program's exit from the body does not stop it either. In the server role any client can do this after one unmasked frame; in the client role a server in `net` can. The queue byte bound of §17.286 (4) is intact; this is the buffer under it. *Server* (`serveHttp` 5148–5263, `rawResponse` 5271, `wsAcceptOn` 5422, `websocket.sak` 132–171, 460–474): (a) `handshake` is pure (`values` and `tokens` over `req.headers`, built from `rawHeaders` so repeats are visible), one string per refusal, used by `host()` and `scripted` through `admitted`. (b) `origins` is matched exactly after `ascii_lower` on both sides; `Some(o)` not in the list refuses, `None` admits; the empty default refuses every browser, `origin: null` included. (c) `rawResponse` writes the status line, the handler's headers through `validateHeaderName`/`Value` with `connection`, `content-length` and `transfer-encoding` dropped, then its own `content-length` and `connection: close`, and echoes no request header. (d) the 101 is `upgrade`, `connection`, `sec-websocket-accept`, `sec-websocket-protocol` when chosen (a `TOKEN`), then `Upgrade.headers` after the `WS_OWN`/`sec-websocket-*` refusal and Node's validation; values pass as latin1, which Node's check confines to `\t`, 0x20–0x7e and 0x80–0xff. (e) one parser with `masked !== s.server` → 1002, `wsOut` masks in the client role only, no extension echoed in either role. (f) `maxSockets()` runs at `serveHttp`'s start (a bad value is this run's `D091` before `listen`), `wsReserve` counts both roles and connects in flight, and at the limit `accept` leaves the connection un-upgraded so the handler's 503 reaches the client. (g) `topics` is one `Map` per process (one instance today), `wsFree` leaves every topic, `ws_publish` is one `write` per subscriber with `wsSkips` (closing, closed, over `max_message`, `writableLength >= max_message`) and no wait. (h) the `Accept` strings carry the origin or subprotocol the peer sent and the host's fixed sentences; Node's validation error names the program's own header. (i) `upgrades` is keyed by the task `serve_listen` made, deleted when it ends; `wsAcceptOn` refuses `conn === undefined`, `conn.upgraded` and `conn.key !== hs.key`, reserves a slot, then sets `upgraded` before writing; the WASM host hands the same function its `served.get(task).conn`. (j) none. **A nit:** `rawResponse` writes whatever `status` the handler returned (`HTTP/1.1 99 `), where the plain path's `writeHead` throws and the request is `D091`/500. *Crates* (`Cargo.toml` 99–113, `Cargo.lock`, `THIRD_PARTY.md`): `aes-gcm` 0.11.1 (`aes`, `alloc`), `p256` 0.14.0 (`ecdsa`, `ecdh`; `elliptic-curve` zeroizes `SecretKey` unconditionally), `ed25519-dalek` 3.0.0 and `x25519-dalek` 3.0.0 (`static_secrets`), default features off, exact pins; the notices file has every crypto row including the transitive `curve25519-dalek` and `zeroize`, gated by `tests/third_party.rs`. In the lock neither dalek crate nor `curve25519-dalek` nor `aes-gcm` depends on `zeroize`: each crate's `zeroize` feature is off, and it is that feature which makes `SigningKey`, its `ExpandedSecretKey`, `StaticSecret` and the AES round keys zero on drop; `rt::crypto` wraps its inputs in `Zeroizing` (§17.288 (7)) and the crates copy them out (`SigningKey::from_bytes(&s)`, `StaticSecret::from(*s)`, `new_from_slice(key)`) into values that are freed as they are. `static_secrets` is the only constructor from bytes, so it is right. *7c* (`sakura_runtime.js` 2785–2840, `crypto.sak` 174–190, 326–331, 536–560, 947–1012, 1225–1240): `oaepSeal` is `lHash = H(L)`, `DB = lHash ‖ PS ‖ 01 ‖ M`, `dbMask = MGF1(seed, k − hLen − 1)`, `maskedDB`, `seedMask = MGF1(maskedDB, hLen)`, `maskedSeed`, `EM = 00 ‖ maskedSeed ‖ maskedDB`, `k` bytes, then `publicEncrypt` with `RSA_NO_PADDING`; `DB`, the masked seed and `EM` are zeroed after; `seal_error` has already refused a seed that is not `hash_len` bytes and a message over `k − 2hLen − 2`, so `Buffer.alloc` never sees a negative; `oaepOpen` is OpenSSL's constant-time unpad and every failure is one `Padding`. The doc says a seed is "fresh" and that a repeat shows two plaintexts equal; it does not say a seed must be unpredictable, and a counter seed, fine for AES-GCM, makes RSA-OAEP a deterministic scheme whose ciphertexts an attacker confirms by sealing their own guess. RSA import: `rsa_parts` reads one SPKI and one PKCS #8 shape, `rsa_der(parts) != b` refuses every non-canonical byte, the modulus is 2,048–16,384 bits, `e` odd, above 1, at most 8 bytes, JWK integers minimal with no `oth`; a private key must produce a signature its own public key verifies (`crypto_public_of`), which proves `(n, e, d)` and nothing about `p`, `q`, `dp`, `dq`, `qi`: OpenSSL's CRT result is checked against `e` and recomputed with `d` when wrong, so a key with any wrong CRT member imports, works, and runs the slow path forever, while Web Crypto's `RSA_check_key` refuses it, so an exported copy fails in a browser. `generate_key_pair` on native for P-384/P-521 is `D090` because the function returns no `Result`, and the `.native.stdout` files declare it. The cost numbers are two now: `crypto_hmac_rfc4231`'s WASM module 366,539 → 418,657 (7b) → 620,973 bytes (7c), its emitted JS 33,856 → 63,108 → 108,125, every program that imports any key paying for every reader `import_key` can reach through a runtime `Algorithm`. The `V9001`: `check` says "No problems" and `run` (JS and WASM) fails `def #6: call row has unbound row variable r0` (`validate.rs:459`) with the span at 1:1; it needs both a `.map(fn(_) { () })` inside a `let`-bound lambda and a call of that lambda from a second lambda; either alone runs (`Ok(())`, `Ok(1)`/`Ok(2)`). Decision: **(1) WebSocket client: approved with fix F1.** Items (a)–(k) hold as listed above. F1, `sakura_runtime.js` WebSocket section and `websocket.test.js`, before the beta.1 preparation commit: `wsData` returns without appending once `s.closed !== null`; `wsEnd` arms `s.timer = setTimeout(() => s.socket.destroy(), WS_CLOSE_MS)` (unref'd) after `end()` unless the socket is already destroyed; `wsFree` does the same after its `end()`. The RFC's rule is kept (the server's FIN is waited for, a bounded time), and the held bytes after a close are none. Acceptance: two `websocket.test.js` cases, one per role, in which the peer sends a close frame (client role: the test server; server role: a raw client after an unmasked frame's 1002) and then 1 MiB more without closing TCP, asserting the peer observes the connection closed within `WS_CLOSE_MS` + 1 s and that no byte is held (a test-only export such as `wsSkips` is acceptable to read `s.buf.length`); the existing close and 1001 cases unchanged; `CHANGELOG.md` Fixed, one line. **(2) WebSocket server: approved with F1 and nit F2.** Items (a)–(j) hold; the 8s readings (1)–(11) are ratified as built, (5) in particular (Node sends a bare 101 the client cannot use, so `serveHttp`'s own check is right). F2, same file and test: `rawResponse` throws before writing when `status` is not an integer in 100..=999, so the raw path is `D091`/500 as the plain one; one test (a handler returning status 99 on an upgrade request gets 500 with `connection: close`). (c)'s "no request header echoed" and (h) stand; the owner's signature items of §17.286 (5) are untouched. **(3) The crate set: approved; F3 enables `zeroize`.** `compiler/Cargo.toml` adds `"zeroize"` to the feature lists of `ed25519-dalek`, `x25519-dalek` and `aes-gcm`; the `Cargo.lock` hunk is dependency-list lines only (`zeroize` under those crates, `curve25519-dalek`, `aes`, `ghash`, `polyval` as their features require), no new package, so `THIRD_PARTY.md` and its test do not move. Acceptance: `cargo tree -p sakura_rt --features native -i zeroize -e features` shows the three direct crates among `zeroize`'s dependents; `git diff --stat Cargo.lock` touches no `[[package]]` block but existing ones' `dependencies`; `cargo test --workspace --locked` and the native corpus green; one `build(rt)` commit, now, not a tag gate (native is off them, §17.245 (2)). `default-features = false` also drops the dalek `precomputed-tables`, a speed choice, which is fine on an experimental backend and is recorded, not changed. **(4) Phase 7c: approved; F4 now, F5 in beta.N; readings ratified; no split; the `V9001` is F6 in beta.N.** `oaepSeal` is approved as read. F4, `crypto.sak`'s `encrypt` doc comment and RFC 0002 §2.7's OAEP clause (Sol: the stdlib page), one sentence: "an RSA-OAEP seed must be unpredictable as well as fresh (`Random.bytes(n)`, never a counter): a seed an attacker can guess lets them confirm a guessed plaintext by sealing it themselves". F5, `sakura_runtime.js`'s `crypto_public_of` RSA branch and `crypto_rsa_key_formats.sak`: after the pairwise check, read the key's JWK (`key.export({ format: "jwk" })`), convert the eight members with `BigInt`, and answer no bytes unless `p·q = n`, `dp = d mod (p − 1)`, `dq = d mod (q − 1)` and `qi·q ≡ 1 (mod p)`; acceptance: the fixture gains a PKCS #8 whose `qi` differs from the Wycheproof key's by one byte and prints `Malformed` on JS and WASM (`.native.stdout` unchanged, `Unavailable`), a `runtime.test.js` case on `crypto_public_of`, and every existing RSA vector still imports; not a beta.1 gate (the importer holds the key; the consequence is interoperation and speed, not secrecy). Ratified: `KeyReason.Unavailable(String)` and `CryptoReason.Unsupported(String)`/`Padding` (`V1001` leaves no other name); `crypto_tier2()` checked first so native reaches no tier-2 primitive; RSA keys import-only (Node's generation is not seedable, so a pair under `Random.seeded` could not be the same bytes everywhere, and a prime search in std is a second RSA to review); `D090` on native for a P-384/P-521 pair (a declared difference under RFC §7, loud, with no `Result` to carry it); the seed-as-nonce and label-as-`aad` shape; PSS salt = hash length; P-384 SHA-384, P-521 SHA-512; AES-KW `key_ops`; `aad` to an algorithm without one `D020`; ABI 1.11.0. The reachability cost is accepted without a split: the RFC names one `import_key` and Web Crypto has one, a module's byte size is paid at load and not per call, and the mechanism that removes it is the one §17.288 (8) named, pruning a `match` on a constructor-literal argument at the call site, which serves every std function; the two measurements above are that row's evidence and it opens in `performance-r1.md` §4.1 at the perf lane's next edit, after 1.0's must-land set, exit under the bucket rule on `crypto_hmac_rfc4231`'s module bytes. F6, `sakura_core/src/lower` (the call-row construction for a call through a `let`-bound lambda from inside another lambda; `validate.rs:459` is the detector, not the fault) with the `V9001` span moved from 1:1 to the def's: acceptance is the repro as `tests/semantics/lambda_calls_lambda_through_result_map.sak` printing `Ok(())` twice on three backends and in `--json`, `check` and `run` agreeing, and the LIR corpus regenerated if a snapshot moves; first in the beta.N queue of §17.292, before the tag if the core lane is idle, since it changes no ABI and no contract. Why: every list item was read at its line, and the one finding is the kind a list cannot surface (the bytes under a bound the list names); the `zeroize` decision follows §17.288 (7)'s own reasoning to the crate boundary at zero new entries; OAEP's doc gap is the difference between a nonce's two properties, which GCM's rule hides; the CRT check is a parity fix with BoringSSL, not a secrecy fix, so it waits; the size question is answered by where the fix belongs, not by the number. Rejected: blocking the beta on F5 or F6 (neither is a secrecy loss or a wrong promise); a split `import_rsa_key` (a name no one asked for, inside the last breaking window, for a cost the compiler should remove); `zeroize` on `p256` (already unconditional in `elliptic-curve`); a runtime read of `NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED` to refuse it (the process owner's variable; a program cannot know whether its operator meant it, and `fetch` would still honour it); destroying the socket at once in `wsEnd` (RFC 6455 §7.1.1 has the server close first and the client wait; the bounded wait keeps that). Performance: F1 is one timer per socket close; F2 one comparison; F3 one `fill` per dropped key struct; F4 none; F5 four `BigInt` operations at import; F6 none.
